لازم.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَازِم (lāzim, 'necessary, obligatory, inseparable, adhering closely'), active participle of لَزِمَ (lazima, 'to cling to, be necessary or obligatory for'); in spoken Arabic, grammaticalized as an invariant modal particle meaning 'must, have to, need to'.

history.meaning: clinging, necessary, obligatory; (modal) must, have to

morphemes.meaning: clinging to, being necessary or obligatory

لافتة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean sign.

لاقى.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'we find it'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

لام.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَامَ (lāma, 'to blame, reproach, censure'), hollow verb from the root ل-و-م (l-w-m, 'blaming, reproaching').

history.meaning: to blame, reproach, find fault with

لامبة.etymology: Variant spelling of لَمْبَة (lamba, 'desk lamp, table lamp, lightbulb'), borrowed via Italian lampa / lampada and French lampe from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch, oil lamp', from λάμπω lámpō 'to shine').

لامع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَامِع (lāmiʿ, 'shining, glossy, gleaming, polished, brilliant'), active participle of لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, flash, gleam').

morphemes.meaning: having a shiny or gleaming quality

لان.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَانَ (lāna, 'to become soft, supple, tender, gentle, yield'), hollow verb from the root ل-ي-ن (l-y-n, 'softness, suppleness, gentleness').

history.meaning: to become soft, pliable, tender, gentle

لباد.etymology: From Classical Arabic لُبَّاد / لِبْد (lubbād / libd, 'wool felt, matted wool'), from لَبَدَ (labada, 'to mat together, press and compact wool into felt, stick fast to the ground'), from the root ل-ب-د (l-b-d).

morphemes.meaning: matting wool together, compacting, sticking fast

لبس.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبِسَ (labisa, 'to wear, put on a garment') and لِبْس / لُبْس (libs / lubs, 'clothing, dress, act of wearing'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *labiš- ('to put on clothes, wear').

لبلاب.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبْلَاب (lablāb, 'ivy, bindweed, climbing vine [Hedera helix or Convolvulus]'), a reduplicated quadriliteral botanical noun shared with Syriac ܠܒܠܒܐ (laḇlāḇā, 'ivy, bindweed'), evoking the plant's twining and wrapping tendrils.

لبن.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَبَن (laban, 'milk; soured milk, yoghurt'), from the Proto-Semitic root *l-b-n ('white', because of the whiteness of milk). In the Levant, لَبَن means specifically 'yoghurt / cultured dairy' (while fresh milk is حَلِيب), whereas in Egypt لبن retains the Classical sense 'milk'.
لبن.notes: The same Semitic root *l-b-n ('white') gave rise to لُبْنَان (Lubnān, 'Mount Lebanon', from its snow-capped white peaks) and لُبَان (lubān, 'frankincense', from its milky-white resin).

لحتى.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean until.

لحد.etymology: Compound preposition لِحَدِّ (li-ḥaddi, 'up to, until, as far as'), formed from the preposition لِـ (li-, 'to') and حَدّ (ḥadd, 'boundary, limit, edge'), from the geminate root ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d).

history.meaning: to the limit of, up to, until

لحظة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَحْظَة (laḥẓa, 'a quick glance of the eye from the outer corner; a moment, instant, blink of an eye'), noun of instance (ism marra) from لَحَظَ (laḥaẓa, 'to glance at, observe').

history.meaning: a single glance of the eye; a brief moment, instant

morphemes.meaning: glancing sideways with the eye, observing
a single glance or fleeting moment

لحظة.notes: Compare English 'in the twinkling of an eye' or German Augenblick ('moment', literally 'eye-glance').

لحق.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَحِقَ (laḥiqa, 'to catch up with, overtake, reach in time, follow closely'), Form I verb from the root ل-ح-ق (l-ḥ-q, 'following closely, overtaking, joining').

history.meaning: to overtake, catch up with, reach in time, follow

morphemes.meaning: catching up with, following closely, joining

لحن.etymology: Classical Arabic لَحْن (laḥn, 'melody, musical mode, cadence of voice'), from root ل-ح-ن denoting modulated intonation and song.

لخبطة.etymology: Verbal noun لَخْبَطَة (laḵbaṭa, 'mix-up, confusion, mess, jumble') of the quadriliteral verb لَخْبَطَ (laḵbaṭa, 'to mix up, muddle, confuse'), formed as an expressive consonantal blend of Classical خَلَطَ (ḵalaṭa, 'to mix') and خَبَطَ (ḵabaṭa, 'to strike at random, knock about blindly').

لزاق.etymology: From Arabic لَزَّاق / لِزَاق (lazzāq / lizāq, 'adhesive tape, sticky tape, glue, cement'), on the intensive instrument pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from لَزِقَ (laziqa, 'to stick, adhere, cling'), a classic phonetic variant of لَصِقَ (laṣiqa).

history.meaning: that which sticks fast; adhesive tape, glue

morphemes.meaning: substance or strip that sticks strongly

لزق.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَزِقَ (laziqa, 'to stick, cling, adhere') and Form II لَزَّقَ (lazzaqa, 'to stick, paste, tape'), recorded by classical Arab philologists as a dialectal and phonological variant of لَصِقَ (laṣiqa, 'to adhere').

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَعَّلَ (Form I and Form II verb)
morphemes.meaning: to adhere or cause to adhere

لسا.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian temporal adverb لِسَّا / لِسَّة (lissā / lissa, 'still, yet; not yet; just now'), contracted from the Classical prepositional phrase لِلسَّاعَةِ (li-s-sāʿati, literally 'up to this hour / up to the present moment').

history.meaning: up to this very hour; still, yet

لسان.etymology: Inherited across Classical and colloquial Arabic from Proto-Semitic anatomical noun *lišān- ('tongue; spoken language'), triliteral root ل-س-ن (l-s-n).
لسان.notes: Masculine in everyday Jordanian (لسانك طويل, 'you have a sharp mouth'), though Classical Arabic allowed both masculine and feminine gender.

لسه.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'still'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

لطف.etymology: Form II causative verb لَطَّفَ (laṭṭafa, 'to make gentle, soften, soothe, lighten [a tense mood]') on the pattern فَعَّلَ (faʿʿala) from لَطُفَ (laṭufa, 'to be delicate, subtle, kind'), triliteral root ل-ط-ف (l-ṭ-f).

history.meaning: to be subtle/kind -> to soften, mitigate
to soften, lighten (especially ألطف الجو, 'lighten the mood')

لطف.notes: Classic social collocation across MSA and Levantine: لطّف الجو ('break the ice / ease the tension in the room').

لطيف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَطِيف (laṭīf, 'kind, gentle, pleasant, gracious, delicate, subtle'), on the adjectival pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from لَطُفَ (laṭufa, 'to be fine, delicate, gentle, kind').

لعاد.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean then / in that case.

لعب.etymology: Form I verb لَعِبَ (laʿiba, 'to play, sport, jest') on the pattern فَعِلَ (faʿila) from the Semitic triliteral root ل-ع-ب (l-ʿ-b, 'playfulness, jesting').

history.meaning: to play, amuse oneself, toy with
to play; with مع in colloquial warnings, 'to mess with'

لعب.notes: Literally 'play', and in Jordanian street/school warnings ما حدا بيلعب معي ('nobody messes with me!') or عم تلعبي بالنار ('you're playing with fire').

لغز.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean and our mystery.

لـ.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean for you (pl.).

لف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, roll up, wind, fold around; [in spoken Arabic also] to turn a corner, go around'), geminate verb from the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f, 'wrapping, winding, turning').

history.meaning: to wrap, roll up, wind; to turn around

لفافة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean rolls of.

لفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَفَّة (laffa, 'a turn, coil, roll, wrap, parcel, sandwich wrap, detour'), noun of instance and concrete noun from لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, roll, turn').

history.meaning: a single turn, roll, wrap, bundle

morphemes.meaning: a single turn or wrapped roll

لفت.etymology: Form I verb لَفَتَ (lafata, 'to turn, twist, bend aside; to turn someone's gaze or mind toward something') inherited from Classical Arabic triliteral root ل-ف-ت (l-f-t, 'turning round, twisting').

history.meaning: to twist, turn someone's face toward or away

rootFamily.gloss: to turn around, look back (Form VIII)
thoughtful gesture, turn of the head

لفت.notes: Almost always appears in the fixed collocations لفت انتباهي ('caught my attention') and لفت نظرهم ('drew their eyes/notice').

لفوق.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'up'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

لفيفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَفِيفَة (lafīfa, 'rolled scroll, bundle, wrapped pastry roll'), on the pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla, passive sense 'that which is rolled or wrapped up') from لَفَّ (laffa, 'to roll up, wrap').

history.meaning: something rolled or wrapped up; scroll, pastry roll

لفّ.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean turn!.

لقاء.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِقَاء (liqāʾ, 'meeting, encounter, reunion, interview'), verbal noun of لَقِيَ (laqiya, 'to meet, encounter') and Form III لَاقَى (lāqā).

لقطة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean bargain / great catch.

لقمة.etymology: From Classical Arabic لُقْمَة (luqma, 'mouthful, bite of food, morsel'), from لَقِمَ (laqima, 'to swallow hurriedly, take a mouthful of food').

morphemes.meaning: taking a mouthful, swallowing a morsel
amount taken in a single bite

لقمة.notes: Borrowed into Turkish as lokma and lokum ('Turkish delight', from راحة الحلقوم / لقمة), and Greek λουκουμάς.

لقى.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَقِيَ (laqiya, 'to meet, encounter, find') and Form III لَاقَى (lāqā, 'to meet, find'), from the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y).

morphemes.part: فَعِلَ / فَاعَلَ (Form I and III verb)

لقي.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'we found'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

لكان.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean then; in that case.

للاسف.etymology: From Classical Arabic لِلْأَسَفِ (li-l-ʾasafi, 'unfortunately, regrettably, to [one's] regret'), prepositional phrase composed of لِـ (li-, 'to, for') + الـ (al-, 'the') + أَسَف (ʾasaf, 'grief, sorrow, regret'), from أَسِفَ (ʾasifa, 'to grieve, feel regret').

لما.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَّا (lammā, 'when, after, as soon as'), temporal conjunction of classical and vernacular Arabic.

لمبة.etymology: From post-Classical Arabic لَمْبَة (lamba, 'lightbulb, lamp, lantern'), borrowed via Italian lampa and Ottoman Turkish lamba from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch, oil lamp', from λάμπω lámpō 'to shine').

لمس.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَسَ (lamasa, 'to touch, feel with the hand') and its verbal noun لَمْس (lams, 'touch, touching'), from the root ل-م-س (l-m-s).

history.meaning: to touch, feel with the hand

لمع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to flash, gleam, glisten'), Semitic root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

لمّع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish, make shine or gleam'), Form II causative of لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, flash, gleam').

history.meaning: to cause to shine, polish, burnish

morphemes.meaning: causative: to make shiny or polish

لهون.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'to here'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

لو.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْ (law, 'if, would that'), conditional and optative particle inherited from Proto-Semitic *law ('if, would that'). Widely used in polite requests such as لَوْ سَمَحْت (law samaḥt, 'if you please / excuse me').

history.meaning: if (hypothetical or polite conditional); would that

لوح.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْح (lawḥ, 'flat board, plank of wood, slate, tablet, sheet or pane of glass/metal'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *lūḥ- ('wooden or stone tablet, plank, board').

history.meaning: board, plank, tablet, flat sheet or pane

لوحة.etymology: Singulative noun لَوْحَة (lawḥa, 'a single board, painting, canvas, signboard, brass nameplate, control panel') formed from لَوْح (lawḥ, 'board, tablet, flat panel').

history.meaning: a single board, plaque, sign, painting

لوز.etymology: Ancient Semitic collective noun لَوْز ('almonds'), native to the rocky hillsides of Jordan and the Levant. Borrowed via Andalusi Arabic اللَّوْزَة into Portuguese tramela/alloza.

لون.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْن (lawn, 'colour, hue, tint; kind, sort, dish of food'), from the root ل-و-ن (l-w-n).

لوية.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَوْيَة (lawya, 'a twist, bend, turn, sprain [e.g. of the ankle or wrist]'), noun of instance (ism marra) from لَوَى (lawā, 'to twist, bend, wrench, turn aside').

history.meaning: a single twist, wrench, bend, or sprain

morphemes.meaning: single act or result of twisting

لوين.etymology: Levantine interrogative adverb لَوَيْن (la-wēn, 'where to?, whither?'), compounded from the directional preposition لَـ (la- < إِلَى / لِـ, 'to') and وَيْن (wēn, 'where?', from وَأَيْنَ wa-ʾayna).

ليش.etymology: Levantine and Gulf interrogative adverb لَيْش / لِيش (lēš / līš, 'why?, for what reason?'), contracted from the Classical Arabic prepositional phrase لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ (li-ʾayyi šayʾin, literally 'for what thing?').
ليش.notes: Formed in parallel with ايش (ʾēš < أَيّ شَيْء 'what?') and قديش (qaddēš < قَدْر أَيّ شَيْء 'how much?').

ليل.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَيْل (layl, 'night, nighttime' as a collective/generic), inherited from Proto-Semitic *layliy- ('night').

ليلة.etymology: Singulative noun لَيْلَة (layla, 'a single night; tonight [الليلة]'), formed from the generic/collective لَيْل (layl, 'nighttime').

ليمون.etymology: Entered Arabic from Persian *līmūn* (ultimately of Indo-Aryan/Austronesian citrus origin), and travelled from Arabic into medieval Mediterranean Europe as English 'lemon'.
ليمون.notes: Collective noun in Jordanian Arabic; a single whole lemon is counted as حبة ليمون.

لَمَع.etymology: From Classical Arabic لَمَعَ (lamaʿa, 'to shine, gleam, flash, sparkle'), vocalized Form I verb from the root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ, 'flashing, shining, gleaming').

مألوف.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَأْلُوف (maʾlūf, 'familiar, customary, accustomed, well-known'), Form I passive participle (on pattern مَفْعُول mafʿūl) of أَلِفَ (ʾalifa, 'to become accustomed to, be familiar or friendly with').

morphemes.meaning: that which one is accustomed to

مؤقت.etymology: From Classical and Modern Standard Arabic مُؤَقِّت (muʾaqqit, 'timer, timekeeper') and مُؤَقَّت (muʾaqqat, 'temporary, timed, provisional'), Form II active/passive participle of وَقَّتَ (waqqata, 'to fix a time, set a timer'), denominative from وَقْت (waqt, 'time'), with shift of initial wāw after ḍamma (*muwaqqit > muʾaqqit).

history.meaning: timekeeper, timer; fixed to a set time, temporary

مؤلف.etymology: From Classical Arabic مُؤَلِّف (muʾallif, 'author, writer, musical composer'), Form II active participle of أَلَّفَ (ʾallafa, 'to join together, unite harmoniously, compile or compose a book or musical work'), from the root ء-ل-ف (ʾ-l-f, 'joining together, familiarity').

history.meaning: one who joins elements into a whole; author, composer

ما.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مَا (mā, 'what, that which; not'), from Proto-Semitic *mā, serving in Levantine Arabic both as the verbal negator ('not') and as a relative/conjunctive particle.

مائي.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مَائِيّ (māʾiyy, 'water-based, aquatic') formed from مَاء (māʾ, 'water') + ـِيّ (-iyy), from the Semitic root م-و-ه (m-w-h).

ماخد.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean taking.

مارق.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'passing'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مازن.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean Mazen.

مازورة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic musical terminology from Italian misura ('measure, bar of sheet music'), from Latin mēnsūra ('measuring, measure').

ماسك.etymology: Active participle مَاسِك (māsik, 'holding, grasping') from the verb مَسَكَ (masaka, 'to hold, grasp, seize') on the triliteral root م-س-ك (m-s-k).

ماسورة.etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ماصوره (masura, 'reed bobbin, water spout, pipe'), itself from Persian ماسوره (māsūra, 'reed tube, spool, pipe').

ماشي.etymology: Active participle مَاشٍ / مَاشِي (māšī, 'walking, going') from مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go, proceed') on the root م-ش-ي (m-š-y); in Levantine speech also used to mean 'working smoothly; alright, okay'.

ماضي.etymology: Active participle مَاضٍ / مَاضِي (māḍī, 'passing, bygone, past, last') from the verb مَضَى (maḍā, 'to pass, elapse, go by') on the root م-ض-ي (m-ḍ-y).

ماكن.etymology: Participial adjective مَاكِن (mākin, 'firm, solid, sturdy, well-established') from مَكُنَ (makuna, 'to be firm, strong, solidly fixed') on the root م-ك-ن (m-k-n).

ماكينة.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine and Egyptian Arabic from Italian macchina ('machine, engine, mechanism'), from Latin māchina, from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ (mākhanā).

مال.etymology: Form I hollow verb مَالَ (māla, 'to incline, lean, tilt, bend') from the triliteral root م-ي-ل (m-y-l).

مالح.etymology: Participial adjective مَالِح (māliḥ, 'salty, salted, saline') derived from مِلْح (milḥ, 'salt') via مَلَحَ (malaḥa, 'to salt, be salty') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ح (m-l-ḥ).

مبارح.etymology: Levantine adverb مْبَارِح (mbāriḥ, 'yesterday'), evolved from Classical Arabic البَارِحَة (al-bāriḥa, 'yesterday, last night') with labial assimilation of the definite article al- to m- before b-, from بَرِحَ (bariḥa, 'to pass away, depart'), root ب-ر-ح (b-r-ḥ).

مبتسم.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُبْتَسِم (mubtasim, 'smiling, beaming') from اِبْتَسَمَ (ibtasama, 'to smile'), derived from بَسَمَ (basama, 'to smile gently') on the root ب-س-م (b-s-m).

مبحوح.etymology: Passive participle (مَفْعُول) of Classical Arabic بَحَّ (baḥḥa, 'to be hoarse'), root ب-ح-ح (b-ḥ-ḥ).

مبروز.etymology: Passive participle of Levantine quadriliteral verb بَرْوَز (barwaz, 'to frame'), from برواز (birwāz, 'frame', Persian parvāz).

مبروك.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean congratulations!.

مبسوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَبْسُوط (mabsūṭ, literally 'spread out, expanded, at ease', whence 'happy, glad, pleased, content') from بَسَطَ (basaṭa, 'to spread out, expand, gladden') on the root ب-س-ط (b-s-ṭ).

مبطّن.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic بَطَّنَ (baṭṭana, 'to line the inside of'), root ب-ط-ن (b-ṭ-n, 'belly, interior').

مبلول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَبْلُول (mablūl, 'wetted, moistened, wet') from the geminate verb بَلَّ (balla, 'to wet, moisten') on the root ب-ل-ل (b-l-l).

مبنى.etymology: Noun of place مَبْنًى / مَبْنَى (mabnā, 'building, structure, edifice') derived from the verb بَنَى (banā, 'to build, construct') on the Proto-Semitic root ب-ن-ي (b-n-y).

مبين.etymology: Levantine active participle مْبَيِّن (mbayyin, 'appearing, looking, obvious'), from Form II مُبَيِّن (mubayyin) of بَيَّنَ (bayyana, 'to make clear; [Levantine] to appear, show, be evident') on the root ب-ي-ن (b-y-n).

مبيّن.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean looking; appearing.

متأخر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَأَخِّر (mutaʾaḫḫir, 'lagging behind, delayed, late') on the pattern مُتَفَعِّل (mutafaʿʿil) of تَأَخَّرَ (taʾaḫḫara, 'to stay back, fall behind, be late'), from the Semitic root ء-خ-ر (ʾ-ḫ-r, 'back, behind, after').

history.meaning: to hang back -> coming late, subsequent
late (in arriving or in the hour of the day)

cognates.meaning: late, tardy (from the same Semitic root ʾ-ḫ-r)

متأخر.notes: Works both as an adjective (الوقت متأخر, 'it's late'; أنا متأخرة, 'I'm running late') and uninflected adverbially in Levantine (نمت متأخر, 'I went to sleep late').

متأكد.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَأَكِّد (mutaʾakkid, 'certain, assured, sure') from تَأَكَّدَ (taʾakkada, 'to become certain, ascertain, verify') on the root ء-ك-د (ʾ-k-d, 'firmness, assurance').

متبدّل.etymology: Form V participle of Arabic تَبَدَّلَ (tabaddala, 'to be exchanged or altered'), Semitic root ب-د-ل (b-d-l).

متحمس.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَحَمِّس (mutaḥammis, 'zealous, fired up, enthusiastic, excited') on the pattern مُتَفَعِّل (mutafaʿʿil) of تَحَمَّسَ (taḥammasa, 'to show ardor or zeal'), from Classical حَمَاسَة / حَمَاس ('bravery, fiery ardor'), triliteral root ح-م-س (ḥ-m-s).

morphemes.meaning: Form V active participle ('filled with enthusiasm')

rootFamily.gloss: to excite, fire someone up (Form II)

متحمس.notes: Standard way in both MSA and Jordanian speech to say 'I am excited!' (أنا كتير متحمسة للرحلة).

متدرّب.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean my two apprentices.

متذكر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَذَكِّر (mutaḏakkir, 'remembering, mindful of') from تَذَكَّرَ (taḏakkara, 'to remember, recall, call to mind') on the Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (ḏ-k-r).

متذكّر.etymology: Form V active participle of Arabic تَذَكَّرَ (tadhakkara, 'to recall, remember'), Semitic root ذ-ك-ر (dh-k-r).

متر.etymology: International metric unit مِتْر ('metre', plural أَمْتَار), borrowed in the 19th century from French mètre, itself from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure, rule')—fully naturalized into Arabic broken-plural morphology (متر -> أمتار).

متساوي.etymology: Form VI active participle مُتَسَاوٍ / مُتَسَاوِي (mutasāwī, 'equal, even, uniform, level') from تَسَاوَى (tasāwā, 'to be equal, be level with one another') on the root س-و-ي (s-w-y).

متشابك.etymology: Form VI reciprocal active participle مُتَشَابِك (mutašābik, 'interlacing with one another, tangled') from the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k, 'to weave, net, interlock'). Literally describes strands or lines crossing over and hooking into each other.

متصل.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُتَّصِل (muttaṣil, 'connected, continuous; caller [by telephone]') from اِتَّصَلَ (ittaṣala, 'to be connected, reach, contact, call') on the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

متل.etymology: Spoken Levantine preposition مِتِل (mitil, 'like, just as'), reflecting the regular urban Levantine shift *ṯ > t from Classical Arabic مِثْل (miṯl, 'likeness, similar; like'), root م-ث-ل (m-ṯ-l).

متوازي.etymology: Form VI active participle مُتَوَازٍ / مُتَوَازِي (mutawāzī, 'running parallel to one another') from the root و-ز-ي (w-z-y, 'to be opposite, equal, abreast of'). Standard geometric and everyday term across Arabic for lines, streets, or ropes running side by side.

متواصل.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean continuous.

متوتر.etymology: Form V active participle مُتَوَتِّر (mutawattir, 'drawn taut; tense, nervous') from تَوَتَّرَ (tawattara, 'to be stretched tight, become tense'), denominal from وَتَر (watar, 'bowstring, string, tendon') on the root و-ت-ر (w-t-r).

متين.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَتِين (matīn, 'firm, solid, tough, durable'), verbal adjective from the root م-ت-ن (m-t-n, 'to be strong, firm, back/ridge'). Retained across Levantine Arabic to praise materials, knots, furniture, and ropes that hold up under stress.

مثقوب.etymology: Passive participle مَثْقُوب (maṯqūb, 'pierced, perforated') from the root ث-ق-ب (ṯ-q-b, 'to bore, pierce, penetrate'), cognate with Hebrew נָקַב (nāqav, via metathesis) and Aramaic תְּקַב. Standard across craft, carpentry, and everyday description for anything punched or holed.

مثيل.etymology: Adjective and noun مَثِيل (maṯīl, 'like, peer, equal, match') derived on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from مَثَلَ (maṯala, 'to resemble, be like') on the Semitic root م-ث-ل (m-ṯ-l).

مجاني.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مَجَّانِيّ (majjāniyy, 'free of charge, complimentary, gratis') formed from مَجَّانًا (majjānan, 'for free, gratis'), borrowed from Classical Syriac ܡܓܢ (maggān, 'freely, gratis').

مجفّف.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic جَفَّفَ (jaffafa, 'to dry out, dehydrate'), root ج-ف-ف (j-f-f).

مجهول.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean unknown; mystery.

مجوز.etymology: Levantine colloquial passive participle مُجَوَّز / مجوّز (mjawwaz, 'doubled, paired'), derived from جَوْز (jōz, 'pair'), itself via phonetic shift from Classical Arabic زَوْج (zawj, 'pair, couple'). Used widely in Jordanian craft and everyday speech for doubled knots, double glass, or paired items.

محافظ.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'keeping'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

محامي.etymology: Form III active participle مُحَامٍ / مُحَامِي (muḥāmī, 'defender, advocate, lawyer') from حَامَى (ḥāmā, 'to defend, protect, plead on behalf of') on the root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

محبس.etymology: Noun of instrument/place مِحْبَس / مَحْبِس (miḥbas / maḥbis, 'device that holds back or shuts off flow; shutoff tap, main valve') from حَبَسَ (ḥabasa, 'to hold back, confine, shut off [water]') on the root ح-ب-س (ḥ-b-s).

محتاج.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُحْتَاج (muḥtāj, 'needing, in need of') from اِحْتَاجَ (iḥtāja, 'to need, require, be in want of') on the hollow root ح-و-ج (ḥ-w-j).

محترم.etymology: Form VIII passive participle مُحْتَرَم (muḥtaram, 'respected, honored, respectable, polite') from اِحْتَرَمَ (iḥtarama, 'to respect, honor, revere') on the root ح-ر-م (ḥ-r-m).

محرك.etymology: Form II active participle مُحَرِّك (muḥarrik, 'mover, agitator; motor, engine') from حَرَّكَ (ḥarraka, 'to move, set in motion') on the root ح-ر-ك (ḥ-r-k).

history.meaning: that which sets in motion; motor; engine

محروق.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean blown / burnt.

محطة.etymology: Noun of place مَحَطَّة (maḥaṭṭa, 'halting place, stopping point, station') from the geminate verb حَطَّ (ḥaṭṭa, 'to put down [loads], alight, halt') on the root ح-ط-ط (ḥ-ṭ-ṭ).

محفظة.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'your wallet'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

محفور.etymology: Form I passive participle مَحْفُور (maḥfūr, 'dug, carved, engraved') from the verb حَفَرَ (ḥafara, 'to dig, carve, engrave, hollow out') on the Semitic root ح-ف-ر (ḥ-f-r).

محكم.etymology: Form IV passive participle مُحْكَم (muḥkam, 'made firm, tightly fitted, well-constructed, snug') from أَحْكَمَ (ʾaḥkama, 'to make firm, tight, sound, or exact') on the root ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m).

محل.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَحَلّ (maḥall, 'place, halting spot, establishment'), noun of place from حَلَّ (ḥalla, 'to alight, settle').

محمي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَحْمِيّ (maḥmiyy, 'protected, guarded, sheltered') from the verb حَمَى (ḥamā, 'to protect, defend, shield') on the root ح-م-ي (ḥ-m-y).

مخبز.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean the bakery.

مخبى.etymology: Levantine Form II passive participle مْخَبَّى (mḫabbā, 'hidden, tucked away') from خَبَّى (ḫabbā, 'to hide'), reflecting the regular Levantine loss of final hamza from Classical Arabic مُخَبَّأ (muḫabbaʾ) of خَبَّأَ (ḫabbaʾa, 'to hide, conceal'), root خ-ب-ء (ḫ-b-ʾ).

مخبّى.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean hidden.

مخبّي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean hiding / keeping secretly.

مختوم.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean stamped; sealed.

مخدة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِخَدَّة ('pillow, cushion', plural مَخَدَّات) built with prefix مِـ on خَدّ ('cheek', geminate root خ-د-د): literally 'a cheek-rest' on which a sleeper lays their cheek.

مخطط.etymology: Passive participle مُخَطَّط ('floor plan, blueprint, layout; striped') from Form II خَطَّطَ ('draw lines, map out'), built on the geminate root خ-ط-ط ('carve or draw a line, خط').

مخفي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَخْفِيّ (maḫfiyy, 'hidden, concealed, kept out of sight') from خَفَى (ḫafā) / خَفِيَ (ḫafiya, 'to hide, be hidden') on the root خ-ف-ي (ḫ-f-y).

مدام.etymology: Borrowed from French madame ('madam, Mrs., ma'am'), originally the phrase ma dame ('my lady'), from Latin mea domina.

مدة.etymology: Noun مُدَّة (mudda, 'stretch of time, period, duration') derived from the geminate verb مَدَّ (madda, 'to stretch, extend, prolong') on the root م-د-د (m-d-d).

مدح.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَدَحَ (madaḥa, 'to praise, commend, eulogize'), root م-د-ح (m-d-ḥ).

مدخل.etymology: Noun of place مَدْخَل (madḫal, 'place of entry, entrance, doorway, lobby') derived from دَخَلَ (daḫala, 'to enter, go in') on the root د-خ-ل (d-ḫ-l).

مدرسة.etymology: Noun of place مَدْرَسَة (madrasa, 'place of study, school') derived from دَرَسَ (darasa, 'to study, learn, read repeatedly') on the Semitic root د-ر-س (d-r-s).

مدفوع.etymology: Form I passive participle مَدْفُوع (madfūʿ, 'pushed, handed over; paid') from دَفَعَ (dafaʿa, 'to push, hand over, pay [a sum]') on the root د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ).

مدهون.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean painted.

مدور.etymology: Form II passive participle مُدَوَّر (mudawwar, 'made round, circular, round') from دَوَّرَ (dawwara, 'to make round, turn around') on the hollow root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

مدوّر.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean round.

مدير.etymology: Form IV active participle مُدِير (mudīr, 'one who turns, runs, or directs; director, manager') from أَدَارَ (ʾadāra, 'to turn, revolve, manage, direct') on the root د-و-ر (d-w-r).

مديرة.etymology: Feminine (-ة) of Form IV active participle مُدِير (mudīr, 'director, manager, principal', literally 'one who makes affairs revolve and run') of أَدَارَ (ʾadāra, 'to turn round, administer, manage'), from the hollow root د-و-ر (d-w-r, 'to revolve, turn in a circle').

history.meaning: to cause to revolve -> overseer, governor

مديرة.notes: Standard across MSA and spoken Jordanian for a female school principal (مديرة المدرسة) or company director.

مدينة.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna, 'city, town'), borrowed from or cognate with Aramaic ܡܕܝܢܬܐ (məḏīntā, 'jurisdiction, province, city'), from the Semitic root د-ي-ن (d-y-n, 'to judge, govern').

مدّد.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean to extend (f.).

مر.etymology: Form I geminate verb مَرَّ (marra, 'to pass, go by, cross') from the Semitic root م-ر-ر (m-r-r).

مراجعة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean review; inspection.

مراية.etymology: Levantine noun مْرَايَة (mrāye, 'mirror, looking-glass'), reshaped from Classical Arabic مِرْآة (mirʾāh, 'mirror'), a noun of instrument derived from رَأَى (raʾā, 'to see') on the root ر-ء-ي (r-ʾ-y).

مربع.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُرَبَّع (murabbaʿ, 'four-sided, quadrangular; square') from رَبَّعَ (rabbaʿa, 'to make four-sided or square'), derived from أَرْبَعَة (ʾarbaʿa, 'four') on the Semitic root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ).

مربوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْبُوط (marbūṭ, 'tied, bound, fastened, attached') from رَبَطَ (rabaṭa, 'to tie, bind, fasten') on the root ر-ب-ط (r-b-ṭ).

مربى.etymology: Passive participle of Form II رَبَّى (rabbā, 'to nurture, cure, preserve in syrup'), from root ر-ب-و: fruit preserved slowly in sugar.

history.meaning: fruit preserve; confection cured in honey or sugar

مرة.etymology: Noun of instance (ism marra) مَرَّة (marra, 'one passing, one time, turn, occasion') from the geminate verb مَرَّ (marra, 'to pass, go by') on the root م-ر-ر (m-r-r).

مرتاح.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُرْتَاح (murtāḥ, 'resting, at ease, relaxed, comfortable') from اِرْتَاحَ (irtāḥa, 'to rest, find relief, feel at ease') on the hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

مرتب.etymology: Form II passive participle مُرَتَّب (murattab, 'arranged in order, organized, neat, tidy') from رَتَّبَ (rattaba, 'to arrange, put in order, tidy up') on the root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b).

مرتبان.etymology: Beloved Levantine pantry word مَرْتَبَان (also spelled مَرْطَبَان, 'glass or glazed storage jar'), named after the historic Burmese port city of Martaban (Mottama), whose glazed stoneware jars carried spices, preserves, sugar, and pickles across Indian Ocean and Ottoman trade routes into Syrian and Jordanian kitchens.

history.meaning: glazed spice and preserve jar from Martaban

مرجاني.etymology: Nisba colour adjective derived from مَرْجَان (marjān, 'coral, small pearls'), a pre-Islamic cultural loan in Arabic connected with Aramaic מַרְגָּנִיתָא (margānīṯā) and Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs, 'pearl'). In modern Jordanian colour usage, مرجاني names the warm pinkish-orange shade of Red Sea coral.

مرحبا.etymology: Adverbial accusative greeting مَرْحَبًا (marḥaban, 'welcome!, hello!'), elliptical for صَادَفْتَ أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا وَمَرْحَبًا ('you have found welcoming kin, smooth ground, and ample room'), from مَرْحَب (marḥab, 'wide, spacious place') on the root ر-ح-ب (r-ḥ-b, 'to be wide, roomy, welcoming').

مرحلة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic noun of place and distance مَرْحَلَة (marḥala, originally 'a single day's journey between two caravan halting-stations') on the pattern مَفْعَلَة (mafʿala) from the triliteral root ر-ح-ل (r-ḥ-l, 'to saddle a camel, set out on a journey').

history.meaning: stage, phase, educational level, breaking point

مرحلة.notes: Links directly to رحلة ('school trip'): every مرحلة ('phase, stage') was originally one leg of a desert journey.

مرخي.etymology: Passive participle مَرْخِيّ (marḫiyy) of the weak-final verb رَخَى / أرخى ('to slacken, loosen, let hang down'), from the root ر-خ-و (r-ḫ-w, 'to be soft, loose, slack'). Directly contrasts with مشدود ('pulled tight') in Levantine speech.

مرسل.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'sender'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مرسوم.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْسُوم (marsūm, 'traced, drawn, sketched, painted') from رَسَمَ (rasama, 'to trace, draw, sketch, mark out') on the root ر-س-م (r-s-m).

مرطبان.etymology: From post-classical Arabic مَرْطَبَان (marṭabān, 'glazed storage vessel, jar'), named after the Mon port city of Martaban (Mottama) in Lower Burma (Myanmar), a major Indian Ocean export center for glazed storage jars that entered Levantine and Ottoman usage for any glass or ceramic food jar.

مرفوع.etymology: Form I passive participle مَرْفُوع (marfūʿ, 'raised, lifted, elevated, propped up') from رَفَعَ (rafaʿa, 'to raise, lift, elevate') on the root ر-ف-ع (r-f-ʿ).

مرق.etymology: Form I verb مَرَقَ (maraqa, 'to pass rapidly through, pierce through'), which in Levantine Arabic (presumably reinforced by Aramaic substrate usage) became the everyday verb meaning 'to pass by, walk past, go through, drop by' on the root م-ر-ق (m-r-q).

history.meaning: to pass by; walk past; drop by

مرقة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean and the broth.

مرقم.etymology: Form II passive participle مُرَقَّم (muraqqam, 'numbered, striped, marked with figures') from the root ر-ق-م (r-q-m, 'to mark, write, number'). Used across both formal Arabic and colloquial Levantine for sequentially numbered pages, tickets, or lantern frames.

مرقّم.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic رَقَّمَ (raqqama, 'to mark with numbers'), from رَقْم (raqm, 'numeral'), root ر-ق-م.

مروحة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِرْوَحَة ('fan, ventilator') formed on the pattern مِفْعَلَة from the hollow root ر-و-ح ('blow gently, breeze, refresh'), originally naming a woven palm-leaf hand fan and in modern Arabic any electric cooling fan.

مريح.etymology: Form IV active participle مُرِيح (murīḥ, 'giving rest, restful, comfortable, soothing') from أَرَاحَ (ʾarāḥa, 'to give rest, relieve, comfort') on the hollow root ر-و-ح (r-w-ḥ).

مريول.etymology: Traditional Levantine noun مَرْيُول (maryūl, 'apron, pinafore, school smock'), considered either an old Mediterranean borrowing linked to Italian/Romance mariola or an expressive colloquial formation for a front-covering garment. Widely used in Jordan for both art/kitchen aprons and classic school pinafores.

مزبوط.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean straight; right.

مزح.etymology: Verbal noun of Classical Arabic مَزَحَ (mazaḥa, 'to jest, joke'), Semitic root م-ز-ح (m-z-ḥ).

مزدوج.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean double.

مزعج.etymology: Form IV active participle مُزْعِج (muzʿij, 'disturbing, unsettling, annoying, noisy') from أَزْعَجَ (ʾazʿaja, 'to disturb, unsettle, trouble, bother') on the root ز-ع-ج (z-ʿ-j).

مزهرية.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean vase.

مزيّت.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean oiled.

مس.etymology: Borrowed in Jordanian and Levantine school usage from English Miss (originally clipped in 17th-century English from mistress), generalized in Amman schools as the respectful everyday title for any female teacher or principal regardless of marital status.

morphemes.meaning: Miss / Ms., female teacher (< English Miss)

history.meaning: polite form of address for a woman or female schoolteacher
female teacher, headmistress (title and common noun)

cognates.meaning: title for a female teacher (source word)

rootFamily.gloss: the female teacher (definite noun in Jordanian student talk)

مس.notes: Colloquial Jordanian school register (contrasting with formal MSA أستاذة or معلمة): takes the Arabic vocative particle (يا مس!), definite article (إجت المس, 'the teacher came'), and precedes first names (مس فاتن).

مسؤولية.etymology: Abstract noun formed in 19th-century Nahda Arabic with the productive suffix -يَّة (-iyya) on Classical passive participle مَسْؤُول (masʾūl, 'questioned, answerable, accountable', pattern مَفْعُول of سَأَلَ saʾala, 'to ask, call to account', root س-ء-ل), calquing French responsabilité.

history.meaning: asked, answerable (cf. Qurʾan 17:36 كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْؤُولًا)

مسؤولية.notes: Spelled مسؤولية (with hamza on و, Jordanian/Gulf/Levant standard) or مسئولية (Egyptian orthography, hamza on ي carrier).

مسا.etymology: Spoken Levantine form مَسَا (masā, 'evening'), with regular drop of word-final hamza after a long vowel from Classical Arabic مَسَاء (masāʾ, 'evening'), root م-س-و (m-s-w).

مساء.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean evening.

مسائي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean evening (adj.).

مسافة.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَسَافَة (masāfa, 'distance, stretch of journey'), noun of place from the hollow root س-و-ف (s-w-f, originally 'to smell/scent the trail', hence the stretch of desert a guide covers by scenting landmarks). Today it is the universal Arabic word for distance and spacing.

مسافر.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic سَافَرَ (sāfara, 'to travel'), root س-ف-ر (s-f-r, 'to set out on a journey').

مستحيل.etymology: Form X active participle مُسْتَحِيل (mustaḥīl, 'altered from its nature, absurd, impossible') from اِسْتَحَالَ (istaḥāla, 'to change state, become impossible or inconceivable') on the hollow root ح-و-ل (ḥ-w-l).

مستعجل.etymology: Form X active participle مُسْتَعْجِل (mustaʿjil, 'hastening, in a hurry, rushing') from اِسْتَعْجَلَ (istaʿjala, 'to hasten, urge speed, be in a hurry') on the root ع-ج-ل (ʿ-j-l).

مستقبل.etymology: Form X passive participle of Arabic اِسْتَقْبَلَ (istaqbala, 'to face, receive what is coming'), root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

مستقيم.etymology: Form X active participle of Arabic اِسْتَقَامَ (istaqāma, 'to stand straight, be upright'), root ق-و-م (q-w-m).

مستوي.etymology: Form VIII participle of Arabic اِسْتَوَى (istawā, 'to become even, level, or mature'), root س-و-ي (s-w-y).

مسجل.etymology: Form II passive participle مُسَجَّل (musajjal, 'registered, recorded, entered in a register') from سَجَّلَ (sajjala, 'to register, record'), denominal from سِجِلّ (sijill, 'scroll, register'), root س-ج-ل (s-j-l).

مسح.etymology: Form I verb مَسَحَ (masaḥa, 'to wipe, rub off, stroke, anoint') from the Proto-Semitic root م-س-ح (m-s-ḥ).

مسطح.etymology: Form II passive participle مُسَطَّح (musaṭṭaḥ, 'flattened, flat, plane') from the root س-ط-ح (s-ṭ-ḥ, 'to spread out flat, level'). Directly related to سَطْح (saṭḥ, 'flat roof, surface'), a hallmark feature of Levantine stone houses.

مسطرة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْطَرَة ('ruler, straightedge', plural مَسَاطِر) formed with prefix مِـ from the root س-ط-ر ('rule straight lines, write in neat rows').

مسطّح.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean flat.

مسك.etymology: Form I verb مَسَكَ (masaka, 'to take hold of, grasp, hold, seize') on the triliteral Semitic root م-س-ك (m-s-k).

مسكة.etymology: Noun مَسْكَة (maska, 'grip, hold; handle, knob, catch [of a door, window, or drawer]') derived from مَسَكَ (masaka, 'to hold, grasp') on the root م-س-ك (m-s-k).

مسكر.etymology: Form II passive participle مُسَكَّر / مْسَكَّر (msakkar, 'closed, shut, locked, blocked off') from سَكَّرَ (sakkara, 'to shut, close, lock, dam up') on the Semitic root س-ك-ر (s-k-r, 'to stop up, dam, shut', reinforced in the Levant by Aramaic ܣܟܪ səkhar 'to shut, close').

مسكون.etymology: Form I passive participle مَسْكُون (maskūn, 'inhabited, occupied, dwelt in') from سَكَنَ (sakana, 'to dwell, reside, inhabit') on the Semitic root س-ك-ن (s-k-n).

مسكين.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِسْكِين (miskīn, 'poor, needy, humble, unfortunate'), an ancient Semitic cultural word borrowed via Aramaic ܡܣܟܢܐ (miskēnā) from Akkadian muškēnum ('subject, commoner, poor person'), later aligned by folk and grammatical analysis with the Arabic root س-ك-ن (s-k-n, 'to be still, humble').

مسمار.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْمَار ('nail, metal pin, peg', plural مَسَامِير) formed on the pattern مِفْعَال from the Semitic root س-م-ر ('fasten tightly with nails').

مسند.etymology: Form IV passive participle مُسْنَد (musnad, 'propped up, leaned against, supported') from أَسْنَدَ (ʾasnada, 'to prop up, lean [something] against, support') on the root س-ن-د (s-n-d).

مش.etymology: Levantine and Egyptian negative particle مِش (miš, 'not'), contracted from earlier مَا هُوَ شَيْء (mā huwa šayʾ) / مَا شَيْء ('not a thing') through intermediate مَا هُوَش (mā hūš), used to negate nominal predicates, adjectives, participles, and prepositional phrases.

مشاركة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُشَارَكَة (mušāraka, 'sharing, participation, partnership') from شَارَكَ (šāraka, 'to share with, take part in, participate') on the root ش-ر-ك (š-r-k).

مشبك.etymology: Noun of instrument مِشْبَك (mišbak, 'clasp, clip, catch, fastener') derived from شَبَكَ (šabaka, 'to entwine, fasten, hook together') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشبوك.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْبُوك (mašbūk, 'fastened, clipped, hooked together, plugged in') from شَبَكَ (šabaka, 'to intertwine, fasten, connect') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشبّك.etymology: Form II passive participle مُشَبَّك (mušabbak, 'fastened with a clip, lattice-worked, clipped') from شَبَّكَ (šabbaka, 'to interlace, fasten together, clip') on the root ش-ب-ك (š-b-k).

مشتر.etymology: Form VIII active participle مُشْتَرٍ (muštarin, construct/definite مُشْتَرِي muštarī, 'buyer, purchaser, customer') from اِشْتَرَى (ištarā, 'to buy, purchase') on the root ش-ر-ي (š-r-y).

مشدود.etymology: Passive participle مَشْدُود (mašdūd, 'pulled tight, fastened, taut') from the geminate root ش-د-د (š-d-d, 'to bind firmly, pull tight, strengthen'). Used in Levantine Arabic both literally for stretched ropes/wires and figuratively for someone tense or deeply absorbed.

مشرق.etymology: Form IV active participle مُشْرِق (mušriq, 'shining, radiant, bright, sunlit') from أَشْرَقَ (ʾašraqa, 'to rise and shine [of the sun], radiate light') on the root ش-ر-ق (š-r-q).

مشروخ.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean chipped / cracked.

مشغول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْغُول (mašġūl, 'busied, occupied, engaged, taken') from شَغَلَ (šaġala, 'to occupy, keep busy, engage') on the root ش-غ-ل (š-ġ-l).

مشقوق.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْقُوق (mašqūq, 'split, cleft, cracked, slit') from the geminate verb شَقَّ (šaqqa, 'to split, cleave, crack open') on the root ش-ق-ق (š-q-q).

مشكلة.etymology: Noun مُشْكِلَة (muškila, 'difficulty, dubious matter, problem'), originally the feminine active participle of Form IV أَشْكَلَ (ʾaškala, 'to be ambiguous, intricate, or difficult to resolve') on the root ش-ك-ل (š-k-l).

مشمس.etymology: Form IV active participle مُشْمِس (mušmis, 'sunny, sunlit') from the denominal verb أَشْمَسَ (ʾašmasa, 'to be bright and sunny [of a day]'), derived from شَمْس (šams, 'sun') on the Proto-Semitic root ش-م-س (š-m-s).

مشهور.etymology: Passive participle مَشْهُور (mašhūr, 'widely known, famous, celebrated') on the pattern مَفْعُول (mafʿūl) of شَهَرَ (šahara, 'to make conspicuous, proclaim publicly, unsheathe a sword'), from the Semitic root ش-ه-ر (š-h-r, also yielding شَهْر 'new moon, month', named for its public visibility).

history.meaning: to make publicly known -> renowned, notorious

مشهور.notes: Covers both public celebrity fame and high-school popularity (البنت المشهورة بالمدرسة).

مشوي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَشْوِيّ (mašwiyy, 'roasted, grilled, broiled') from شَوَى (šawā, 'to roast, grill [meat or vegetables]') on the Semitic root ش-و-ي (š-w-y).

مشى.etymology: Form I defective verb مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go on foot, proceed, function smoothly') on the triliteral root م-ش-ي (m-š-y).

مشي.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) مَشْي (mašy, 'walking, going on foot, pace') from the verb مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk') on the root م-ش-ي (m-š-y).

مشية.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'for a walk'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مصاري.etymology: Levantine plural noun مَصَارِي (maṣārī, 'money, cash'), historically the broken plural of مِصْرِيَّة (miṣriyya, 'Egyptian [coin]'), denoting the Ottoman silver para coins minted in Cairo (مِصْر Miṣr) that served as everyday currency across Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan.

مصب.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'spout'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مصدق.etymology: Form II active participle مُصَدِّق / مْصَدِّق (mṣaddiq, 'believing, holding to be true') from صَدَّقَ (ṣaddaqa, 'to believe, deem true, confirm') on the Semitic root ص-د-ق (ṣ-d-q).

مصروف.etymology: Passive participle of ص-ر-ف (s-r-f) on the pattern مفعول, literally 'that which is spent or disbursed', used as a noun for everyday expenses or pocket money.
مصروف.notes: The root ص-ر-ف covers turning, exchanging currency, and spending money.

مصفى.etymology: Form II passive participle مُصَفًّى / مْصَفَّى (mṣaffā, 'strained, filtered, drained, clarified') from صَفَّى (ṣaffā, 'to strain, filter, purify, drain') on the root ص-ف-و (ṣ-f-w).

مصنفر.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean frosted / sandblasted.

مصيبة.etymology: Noun مُصِيبَة (muṣība, 'calamity, misfortune, disaster'), originally the feminine active participle of Form IV أَصَابَ (ʾaṣāba, 'to hit the mark [of an arrow], strike, befall, afflict someone') on the hollow root ص-و-ب (ṣ-w-b).

مصيدة.etymology: Noun of instrument مِصْيَدَة (miṣyada, 'trap, snare, net, hunting device') derived from صَادَ (ṣāda, 'to hunt, catch, trap') on the hollow Semitic root ص-ي-د (ṣ-y-d).

مضبوط.etymology: Form I passive participle مَضْبُوط (maḍbūṭ, pronounced mazbūṭ in urban Levantine with sibilant voicing of ḍ > z via Ottoman Turkish pronunciation, 'held firm, regulated, accurate, exact; properly, right') from ضَبَطَ (ḍabaṭa, 'to hold fast, regulate, render exact') on the root ض-ب-ط (ḍ-b-ṭ).

مضحك.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'funny'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مضغوط.etymology: Passive participle (مَفْعُول) of Classical Arabic ضَغَطَ (ḍaghaṭa, 'to press, compress, squeeze'), root ض-غ-ط (ḍ-gh-ṭ).

مطابق.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic طَابَقَ (ṭābaqa, 'to fit closely, match, correspond'), root ط-ب-ق (ṭ-b-q).

مطبخ.etymology: Noun of place on the pattern مَفْعَل (maf'al) from the Semitic root ط-ب-خ (t-b-kh, 'to cook'), literally 'place of cooking'.
مطبخ.notes: Regular place-noun formation alongside مدخل ('entrance') and مكتب ('office/desk').

مطبوع.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean printed.

مطر.etymology: Inherited Semitic weather noun from م-ط-ر (m-t-r, 'to rain'), cognate with Hebrew *māṭār* and Ugaritic *mṭr*.
مطر.notes: Winter rain (مطر الشتا) feeds Amman's gardens and stone cisterns.

مطرقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِطْرَقَة ('hammer') formed with the tool prefix مِـ (mi-) on the root ط-ر-ق ('to strike, knock, forge metal'). In a piano, the same word names each felt-covered wooden hammer striking the strings.

مطوي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَطْوِيّ (maṭwiyy, 'folded, rolled up, tucked') from طَوَى (ṭawā, 'to fold, roll up') on the root ط-و-ي (ṭ-w-y).

مطّر.etymology: Form II denominal verb مَطَّرَ (maṭṭara, 'to rain, pour down rain'), corresponding to Classical Arabic أَمْطَرَ (ʾamṭara) and مَطَرَ (maṭara), derived from مَطَر (maṭar, 'rain') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ط-ر (m-ṭ-r).

مع.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مَعَ / مَعْ (maʿa / maʿ, 'with, together with, in the company of'), from Proto-Semitic *maʿ- / *ʿim- ('with').

معبّي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean filling.

معتم.etymology: Form IV active participle مُعْتِم (muʿtim, 'darkening, dim, dark, unlit') from أَعْتَمَ (ʾaʿtama, 'to enter into nightfall, become dark'), related to عَتَمَة (ʿatama, 'darkness of night') on the root ع-ت-م (ʿ-t-m).

معجزة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean miracles.

معجنات.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean pastry / baked goods.

معدن.etymology: Noun of place and substance مَعْدِن (maʿdin, 'mine, quarry; mineral, ore, metal') derived from عَدَنَ (ʿadana, 'to remain fixed in the earth, abide in a place') on the root ع-د-ن (ʿ-d-n).

معرش.etymology: Form II active/passive participle مُعَرِّش / مْعَرِّش (mʿarriš, 'climbing on a trellis, trailing over an arbor [of vines]') from عَرَّشَ (ʿarraša, 'to train a vine upon a trellis, roof over with a bower'), denominal from عَرْش / عَرِيش (ʿarīš, 'trellis, pergola, arbor') on the root ع-ر-ش (ʿ-r-š).

معروض.etymology: Form I passive participle مَعْرُوض (maʿrūḍ, 'presented, exhibited, displayed, offered [for sale]') from عَرَضَ (ʿaraḍa, 'to show, present, offer, display') on the root ع-ر-ض (ʿ-r-ḍ).

معصب.etymology: Levantine Form II active participle مْعَصِّب (mʿaṣṣib, 'angry, cross, worked up'), from عَصَّبَ (ʿaṣṣaba, 'to bind tightly; [Levantine, denominal from أَعْصَاب ʾaʿṣāb "nerves"] to get tense, lose one's temper, become angry') on the root ع-ص-ب (ʿ-ṣ-b).

معطف.etymology: Instrumental garment noun مِعْطَف ('coat, overcoat', plural مَعَاطِف) formed with prefix مِـ from the root ع-ط-ف ('bend around, fold over affectionately'), literally 'a garment wrapped warmly around the shoulders'.

معطي.etymology: Form IV active participle مُعْطٍ / مَعْطِي (muʿṭī / maʿṭī, 'giving, having given') from أَعْطَى (ʾaʿṭā, 'to give, grant, hand over') on the root ع-ط-و (ʿ-ṭ-w).

معقول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَعْقُول (maʿqūl, 'comprehended by the mind, reasonable, sensible, plausible; [interjection] really?!, can it be?!') from عَقَلَ (ʿaqala, 'to bind; understand, reason') on the root ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l).

معلق.etymology: Form II passive participle مُعَلَّق (muʿallaq, 'hung, suspended, hanging, attached') from عَلَّقَ (ʿallaqa, 'to hang up, suspend, attach') on the root ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q).

معلقة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean the spoon.

معلم.etymology: Form II active participle مُعَلِّم (muʿallim, 'teacher, instructor; master craftsman, boss') from عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, 'to teach, instruct, train in a craft') on the Semitic root ع-ل-م (ʿ-l-m).

معلّق.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean hanging.

معلّم.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean boss / master.

معماري.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مِعْمَارِيّ (miʿmāriyy, 'architectural; architect') formed from مِعْمَار (miʿmār, 'master builder, mason, architect'), an intensive instrument/agent formation from عَمَرَ (ʿamara, 'to build, construct, inhabit') on the root ع-م-ر (ʿ-m-r).

معنى.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'its meaning (then)'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

معين.etymology: Form II passive participle مُعَيَّن (muʿayyan, 'specified, pinpointed, particular') on the pattern مُفَعَّل (mufaʿʿal) of عَيَّنَ (ʿayyana, 'to fix with the eye, individuate, appoint'), denominative from عَيْن (ʿayn, 'eye; exact self'), hollow root ع-ي-ن (ʿ-y-n).

history.meaning: to specify, appoint -> specified, designated; rhombus

معين.notes: Follows an indefinite noun to render English 'a certain...' (شخص معين 'a certain person', لمرحلة معينة 'up to a certain point').

مغبر.etymology: Form II participle adjective مُغَبَّر (muġabbar, 'covered with dust, dusty') derived from غُبَار / غَبْرَة (ġubār / ġabra, 'dust'), from the root غ-ب-ر (ġ-b-r, 'to be dust-coloured, remain behind'). Common everyday Levantine word after windy days.

مغبش.etymology: Levantine Form II participle مْغَبِّش / مُغَبَّش (mġabbiš, 'blurred, misty, fogged up, frosted [of glass]') from غَبَّشَ (ġabbaša, 'to dim, blur, cloud over'), derived from Classical Arabic غَبَش (ġabaš, 'dimness of twilight before dawn, haziness') on the root غ-ب-ش (ġ-b-š).

مغبّش.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean misty / fogged up.

مغرفة.etymology: Noun of instrument from Classical Arabic غَرَفَ (gharafa, 'to scoop water or soup with the hand or a spoon'), root غ-ر-ف.

مغسلة.etymology: Noun of place مَغْسَلَة (maġsala, 'washing place, washbasin, sink, laundry') derived from غَسَلَ (ġasala, 'to wash') on the root غ-س-ل (ġ-s-l).

مغلف.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُغَلَّف (muġallaf, 'wrapped, encased; envelope') from غَلَّفَ (ġallafa, 'to wrap, encase, put in a cover or envelope'), denominal from غِلَاف (ġilāf, 'cover, wrapper, sheath') on the root غ-ل-ف (ġ-l-f).

مغلّف.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean laminated / wrapped.

مفتاح.etymology: Instrumental noun on the pattern مِفْعال (mif'āl) from the root ف-ت-ح (f-t-h, 'to open'), literally 'an instrument for opening'.
مفتاح.notes: In Jordanian Arabic مفتاح covers both a door key and a mechanic's spanner or wrench.

مفتش.etymology: Form II active participle مُفَتِّش (mufattiš, 'examiner, searcher, inspector') from فَتَّشَ (fattaša, 'to search carefully, examine, inspect') on the root ف-ت-ش (f-t-š).

مفتوح.etymology: Form I passive participle مَفْتُوح (maftūḥ, 'opened, open') from فَتَحَ (fataḥa, 'to open') on the Proto-Semitic root ف-ت-ح (f-t-ḥ).

مفرش.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean tablecloths.

مفرود.etymology: Passive participle of Arabic فَرَدَ (farada, 'to spread out, unfold, flatten'), root ف-ر-د (f-r-d).

مفروض.etymology: Form I passive participle مَفْرُوض (mafrūḍ, 'ordained, imposed, obligatory; supposed [to], expected') from فَرَضَ (faraḍa, 'to notch, appoint, impose as an obligation, suppose') on the root ف-ر-ض (f-r-ḍ).

مفصلة.etymology: Noun of instrument/place مِفْصَلَة / مَفْصَلَة (mifṣala / mafṣala, 'hinge, articulated joint [of a door or shutter]') derived from فَصَلَ (faṣala, 'to separate, divide at a joint'; compare مَفْصِل mafṣil 'anatomical joint') on the root ف-ص-ل (f-ṣ-l).

مفضل.etymology: Form II passive participle مُفَضَّل (mufaḍḍal, 'preferred, favored, favorite') from فَضَّلَ (faḍḍala, 'to prefer, favor, deem superior') on the root ف-ض-ل (f-ḍ-l).

مفقودات.etymology: Feminine sound plural مَفْقُودَات (mafqūdāt, 'lost items, lost property') of the Form I passive participle مَفْقُود (mafqūd, 'lost, missing') from فَقَدَ (faqada, 'to lose, miss') on the root ف-ق-د (f-q-d).

مفك.etymology: Noun of instrument مِفَكّ (mifakk, 'tool for loosening or unscrewing; screwdriver') derived from the geminate verb فَكَّ (fakka, 'to untie, loosen, unfasten, unscrew') on the root ف-ك-ك (f-k-k).

مفكر.etymology: Form II active participle مُفَكِّر / مْفَكِّر (mfakkir, 'thinking, pondering; [Levantine] thinking, supposing') from فَكَّرَ (fakkara, 'to think, reflect, suppose') on the root ف-ك-ر (f-k-r).

مفيد.etymology: Form IV active participle مُفِيد (mufīd, 'beneficial, useful, informative') of أَفَادَ (ʾafāda, 'to confer benefit, profit, or meaning'), built on the hollow triliteral root ف-ي-د (f-y-d, 'benefit, utility').

history.meaning: to impart benefit or complete meaning -> useful, instructive

rootFamily.gloss: benefit, point/use (ما في فايدة = 'it's no use')

مفيد.notes: Fun grammar trivia: in medieval Arabic grammar, جملة مفيدة ('a useful/complete sentence') is the technical term for an independent clause that conveys a complete thought!

مقابل.etymology: Form III active participle مُقَابِل (muqābil, 'facing, opposite, across from, in return for') from قَابَلَ (qābala, 'to face, stand opposite, meet face to face') on the Semitic root ق-ب-ل (q-b-l).

مقاس.etymology: Noun of measure مَقَاس (maqās, 'measurement, dimension, size') derived from the hollow verb قَاسَ (qāsa, 'to measure, gauge, compare') on the root ق-ي-س (q-y-s).

مقام.etymology: Noun of place/standing مَقَام ('standing place, station, musical mode/key') built with prefix مَـ on the hollow root ق-و-م ('stand, rise'). In Arab musical theory since the medieval treatises, مقام names the tonal scale/mode (and by extension a piece's key) on which a melody rests.

مقرمش.etymology: Quadriliteral active participle مُقَرْمِش / مْقَرْمِش (mqarmiš, 'crunchy, crispy, crusty') from قَرْمَشَ (qarmaša, 'to crunch, nibble crisp food'), an expressive quadriliteral expansion of Semitic roots ق-ر-م (q-r-m, 'to gnaw, nibble') and ق-ر-ش (q-r-š, 'to crunch').

مقعد.etymology: Noun of place (مَفْعَد) from root ق-ع-د (q-ʿ-d, 'to sit down'): literally 'a place for sitting', hence a chair seat or garden bench.

مقفول.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean locked.

مقلي.etymology: Form I passive participle مَقْلِيّ (maqliyy, 'fried, roasted in a pan') from قَلَى (qalā, 'to fry, roast') on the Semitic root ق-ل-ي (q-l-y).

مقنطر.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean arched.

مقهى.etymology: Noun of place مَقْهًى ('coffeehouse, café', plural مَقَاهٍ / مقاهي) formed with the locative prefix مَـ from قَهْوَة ('coffee'), literally 'the place where coffee is brewed and shared'.

مقوس.etymology: Form II passive participle مُقَوَّس (muqawwas, 'curved like a bow, arched, vaulted') from قَوَّسَ (qawwasa, 'to bend into an arch or bow'), denominal from قَوْس (qaws, 'bow, arch, arc') on the Proto-Semitic root ق-و-س (q-w-s).

مقوّس.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean arched.

مكالمة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُكَالَمَة (mukālama, 'speaking with someone, conversation; telephone call') from كَالَمَ (kālama, 'to speak with, address, converse') on the root ك-ل-م (k-l-m).

مكان.etymology: Noun of place مَكَان (makān, 'place, spot, location, site'), formed with the locative prefix ma- from كَانَ (kāna, 'to be, exist, stand') on the root ك-و-ن (k-w-n), and secondarily reanalyzed as root م-ك-ن (m-k-n) in its plural أَمَاكِن (ʾamākin).

مكتب.etymology: Noun of place مَكْتَب (maktab, 'place of writing; desk, office, study') derived from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write') on the Semitic root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

history.meaning: place of writing; school; desk; office

مكتبة.etymology: Noun of place مَكْتَبَة (maktaba, 'place of books; library, bookshop, bookcase') formed on the pattern مَفْعَلَة (mafʿala) from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write') and كِتَاب (kitāb, 'book'), root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

مكتوب.etymology: Form I passive participle مَكْتُوب (maktūb, 'written, inscribed, recorded') from كَتَبَ (kataba, 'to write') on the Semitic root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b).

مكرم.etymology: Form II passive participle مُكَرَّم (mukarram, 'honoured, revered, treated generously') from the root ك-ر-م (k-r-m, 'nobility, generosity, honour'). Classic polite hospitality expression across Arabic when welcoming guests.

مكسور.etymology: Form I passive participle مَكْسُور (maksūr, 'broken, fractured, shattered') from كَسَرَ (kasara, 'to break, fracture') on the Semitic root ك-س-ر (k-s-r).

مكشوف.etymology: Form I passive participle مَكْشُوف (makšūf, 'uncovered, exposed, bare, open to the air') from كَشَفَ (kašafa, 'to uncover, reveal, expose') on the root ك-ش-ف (k-š-f).

مكعب.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُكَعب (mukaʿʿab, 'cube-shaped; cube, die') from كَعَّبَ (kaʿʿaba, 'to make cubic'), denominal from كَعْب (kaʿb, 'anklebone, knucklebone die, cube') on the root ك-ع-ب (k-ʿ-b).

مكوي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean ironed.

ملاحظة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُلَاحَظَة (mulāḥaẓa, 'observing, noticing; observation, remark, note') from لَاحَظَ (lāḥaẓa, 'to observe, notice, watch attentively') on the root ل-ح-ظ (l-ḥ-ẓ).

ملاقي.etymology: Form III active participle مُلَاقٍ / مْلَاقِي (mlāqī, 'meeting, encountering; [Levantine] finding') from لَاقَى (lāqā, 'to encounter, meet; [Levantine] to find') on the root ل-ق-ي (l-q-y).

ملح.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic primary noun مِلْح ('salt') from `*milḥ-`, conserved unchanged for millennia across Arabic, Hebrew, and Aramaic—and central to the Arab ethic of hospitality (عيش وملح, 'bread and salt').

ملحن.etymology: Form II active participle مُلَحِّن (mulaḥḥin, 'melodist, musical composer') from لَحَّنَ (laḥḥana, 'to chant, set to music, compose a melody'), denominal from لَحْن (laḥn, 'melody, tune, tone') on the root ل-ح-ن (l-ḥ-n).

ملزق.etymology: Levantine Form II passive participle مْلَزَّق (mlazzaq, 'stuck on, glued, taped') from لَزَّقَ (lazzaqa, 'to stick, glue, tape'), from Classical Arabic لَزِقَ (laziqa, variant of لَصِقَ laṣiqa, 'to adhere, cling, stick') on the root ل-ز-ق (l-z-q).

ملصق.etymology: Form IV passive participle and noun مُلْصَق (mulṣaq, 'affixed, pasted on; sticker, label, poster') from أَلْصَقَ (ʾalṣaqa, 'to stick, affix, paste') on the root ل-ص-ق (l-ṣ-q).

ملعقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْعَقَة ('spoon') formed with prefix مِـ on the root ل-ع-ق ('lick, sip honey or soup'). In spoken Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, harmless metathesis shifts مِلْعَقَة to مَعْلَقَة (ma'laqa).

ملف.etymology: Noun مِلَفّ / مَلَفّ (milaff / malaff, 'wrapper, folder, binder, file, dossier') derived from the geminate verb لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, fold, roll up') on the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

ملفوف.etymology: Form I passive participle مَلْفُوف (malfūf, 'wrapped, rolled up, folded') from the geminate verb لَفَّ (laffa, 'to wrap, roll, fold') on the root ل-ف-ف (l-f-f).

ملقط.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْقَط ('tweezers, tongs') formed with the tool pattern مِفْعَل on the root ل-ق-ط ('pick up, glean tiny things from the ground').

ملكي.etymology: Nisba relational adjective مَلَكِيّ (malakiyy, 'royal, kingly') derived from مَلِك (malik, 'king'), from the pan-Semitic root م-ل-ك (m-l-k, 'to reign, possess, advise'). In modern colour naming it translates 'royal' in shades such as أزرق ملكي ('royal blue').

ملكية.etymology: Abstract noun مِلْكِيَّة (milkiyya, 'ownership, property right, title') formed with the abstract suffix ـِيَّة (-iyya) from مِلْك (milk, 'possession, property, ownership') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ك (m-l-k).

ملمع.etymology: Form II passive participle مُلَمَّع (mulammaʿ, 'polished, burnished, made glossy or shiny') from لَمَّعَ (lammaʿa, 'to polish, burnish, cause to shine') on the root ل-م-ع (l-m-ʿ).

ملى.etymology: Levantine verb مَلَى (malā, 'to fill, fill up'), reflecting the regular Levantine merger of final-hamza verbs into final-yāʾ from Classical Arabic مَلَأَ (malaʾa, 'to fill') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ل-ء (m-l-ʾ).

ملي.etymology: Colloquial clipped form مِلِّي (millī, 'millimetre') of مِلِّيمِتْر (millīmitr, 'millimetre'), borrowed from French millimètre (from Latin mille 'thousand' + Greek μέτρον métron 'measure').

مليان.etymology: Levantine adjective مَلْيَان (malyān, 'full, filled'), reshaped with the glide -y- from Classical Arabic مَلْآن (malʾān, 'full') on the stative pattern فَعْلَان (faʿlān) from مَلَأَ (malaʾa, 'to fill'), root م-ل-ء (m-l-ʾ).

مليمتر.etymology: Borrowed from French millimètre ('millimetre'), formed from Latin mille ('thousand') + Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

ممتاز.etymology: Form VIII participle مُمْتَاز (mumtāz, 'distinguished, set apart, outstanding, excellent') from اِمْتَازَ (imtāza, 'to be distinguished, stand out above others') on the hollow root م-ي-ز (m-y-z).

ممثّل.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean representative.

ممر.etymology: Noun of place (ism makān) on the pattern مَفْعَل (mafʿal) from the geminate root م-ر-ر (m-r-r, 'to pass, go through'), literally 'a place of passing' — a corridor, hallway, or walkway.

ممزوع.etymology: Levantine passive participle مَمْزُوع (mamzūʿ, 'torn, ripped') from colloquial مَزَعَ (mazaʿ, 'to tear cloth or paper'), itself from Classical Arabic مَزَعَ (mazaʿa, 'to pluck apart cotton/wool, rush') blending semantically with مَزَّقَ (mazzaqa, 'to tear to shreds').

ممطر.etymology: Form IV active participle مُمْطِر (mumṭir, 'rainy, bringing rain') from أَمْطَرَ (ʾamṭara, 'to rain, send down rain'), derived from مَطَر (maṭar, 'rain') on the Proto-Semitic root م-ط-ر (m-ṭ-r).

ممكن.etymology: Form IV active participle مُمْكِن (mumkin, 'possible, feasible; [in polite requests] may I?, could?') from أَمْكَنَ (ʾamkana, 'to be possible, enable') on the root م-ك-ن (m-k-n).

ممل.etymology: Form IV active participle مُمِلّ (mumill, 'wearisome, tedious, boring, dull') from أَمَلَّ (ʾamalla, 'to weary, tire, bore') on the geminate root م-ل-ل (m-l-l).

ممنوع.etymology: Form I passive participle مَمْنُوع (mamnūʿ, 'withheld, prevented, forbidden, not allowed') from مَنَعَ (manaʿa, 'to prevent, withhold, forbid') on the root م-ن-ع (m-n-ʿ).

مميز.etymology: Form II passive/active participle مُمَيَّز / مُمَيِّز (mumayyaz, 'distinguished, distinctive, special, signature') from مَيَّزَ (mayyaza, 'to distinguish, single out, set apart') on the hollow root م-ي-ز (m-y-z).

من.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِنْ (min, 'from, of, out of, than'), from Proto-Semitic *min ('from').

مناخير.etymology: Plural of Classical Arabic مِنْخَار / مَنْخَر (minkhār, 'nostril'), root ن-خ-ر, generalized in Levantine and Egyptian Arabic to mean 'nose'.

مناسب.etymology: Form III active participle مُنَاسِب (munāsib, 'corresponding, fitting, suitable, appropriate') from نَاسَبَ (nāsaba, 'to correspond to, suit, be proportionate to') on the root ن-س-ب (n-s-b).

منبه.etymology: Form II active participle and noun مُنَبِّه (munabbih, 'awakener, warner; alarm clock') from نَبَّهَ (nabbaha, 'to awaken, rouse from sleep, alert') on the root ن-ب-ه (n-b-h).

منحوت.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'carved'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

منخار.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'my nose'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مندهش.etymology: Form VII active participle مُنْدَهِش (mundahiš, 'astonished, amazed, surprised') from اِنْدَهَشَ (indahaša, 'to be astonished, taken aback'), derived from دَهِشَ (dahiša, 'to be bewildered, amazed') on the root د-ه-ش (d-h-š).

منديل.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِنْدِيل / مَنْدِيل (mindīl / mandīl, 'kerchief, napkin, hand towel'), borrowed via Byzantine Greek μανδήλιον (mandḗlion) from Late Latin mantēle / mantēlium ('hand towel, napkin', derived from manus 'hand').

منذ.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean for; since.

منشفة.etymology: Instrumental noun on the feminine pattern مِفْعَلَة (mif'ala) from ن-ش-ف (n-sh-f, 'to dry, absorb moisture'), literally 'a drying cloth, towel'.
منشفة.notes: Plural مناشف; directly transparent alongside the adjective ناشف ('dry').

منشور.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean published.

منطقة.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic مِنْطَقَة / مَنْطِقَة (minṭaqa / manṭiqa, originally 'girdle, belt, waist-zone', then geographical 'zone, region, area, district'), derived from نَطَقَ (naṭaqa, 'to gird, encircle') on the root ن-ط-ق (n-ṭ-q).

منظر.etymology: From Classical Arabic مَنْظَر (manẓar, 'sight, view, aspect, scenic vista'), a noun of place (مَفْعَل) from the root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r, 'to look, gaze, behold'). Used across all Arabic varieties for both natural panoramas and striking sights.

منعش.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean bright; refreshing.

منور.etymology: Form II participle مُنَوَّر / مْنَوِّر (mnawwir, 'illuminated, lit up, bright, shining') from نَوَّرَ (nawwara, 'to illuminate, light up, shine'), denominal from نُور (nūr, 'light') on the Semitic root ن-و-ر (n-w-r).

منوّر.etymology: Form II active participle of Arabic نَوَّرَ (nawwara, 'to shine, light up'), from نُور (nūr, 'light'), root ن-و-ر (n-w-r).

منيح.etymology: Levantine adjective مْنِيح (mnīḥ, 'good, fine, well'), formed by liquid-nasal dissimilation (l > n before Labial m-) from Classical Arabic مَلِيح (malīḥ, 'pleasant, comely, good, winsome'), originally 'savory, well-salted' from مِلْح (milḥ, 'salt') on the root م-ل-ح (m-l-ḥ).

مهذب.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'and polite'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

مهرجان.etymology: Early borrowing into Arabic مِهْرَجَان (mihrajān) from Middle Persian Mihragān (the autumn festival of Mithra), now meaning any festival.

مهل.etymology: Verbal noun مَهْل (mahl, 'gentle pace, slowness, deliberation, ease'), used especially in عَلَى مَهْل (ʿalā mahl, 'slowly, gently, take your time'), from مَهَلَ (mahala, 'to proceed gently and without haste') on the root م-ه-ل (m-h-l).

مهم.etymology: Form IV active participle مُهِمّ (muhimm, 'causing concern, momentous, important') from أَهَمَّ (ʾahamma, 'to concern, occupy the mind, matter to') on the geminate root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

مهملات.etymology: Feminine sound plural مُهْمَلَات (muhmalāt, 'discarded things, rubbish, trash') of the Form IV passive participle مُهْمَل (muhmal, 'neglected, left unused, discarded') from أَهْمَلَ (ʾahmala, 'to neglect, leave alone, discard') on the root ه-م-ل (h-m-l).

history.meaning: neglected or discarded items; waste; rubbish

مهندس.etymology: Quadriliteral active participle مُهَنْدِس (muhandis, 'surveyor, geometrician, architect, engineer') from هَنْدَسَ (handasa, 'to measure, lay out water channels or buildings, engineer'), denominal from هَنْدَسَة (handasa, 'geometry, architecture, engineering'), Arabicized from Middle Persian handāzag / Persian اندازه (andāza, 'measure, proportion, plan').

مو.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean not.

موافق.etymology: Form III active participle of Arabic وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree, accord with'), root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

موافقة.etymology: Form III verbal noun مُوَافَقَة (muwāfaqa, 'agreement, consent, approval, accord') from وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree with, suit, consent to') on the root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

موجود.etymology: Form I passive participle مَوْجُود (mawjūd, 'found, existing, present, available') from وَجَدَ (wajada, 'to find') on the Semitic root و-ج-د (w-j-d).

موسيقى.etymology: Borrowed into Classical Arabic مُوسِيقَى (mūsīqā, 'music') from Ancient Greek μουσική [τέχνη] (mousikḗ [tékhnē], 'art of the Muses, music'), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, 'Muse').

موسيقي.etymology: Relational adjective (nisba) مُوسِيقِيّ (mūsīqiyy, 'musical; musician') formed with the suffix ـِيّ (-iyy) from مُوسِيقَى (mūsīqā, 'music'), from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ).

موصول.etymology: Form I passive participle مَوْصُول (mawṣūl, 'joined, connected, linked, wired') from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, connect, link, reach') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

موضة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic from Italian moda / French mode ('fashion, manner'), ultimately from Latin modus ('measure, manner').

موضوع.etymology: Passive participle مَوْضُوع (mawḍūʿ, literally 'placed, laid down') on the pattern مَفْعُول (mafʿūl) of وَضَعَ (waḍaʿa, 'to lay down, set in place'), from the initial-weak root و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ); already used in medieval Arabic logic and rhetoric for a 'subject or proposition laid down for discussion' (parallel to Greek hupokeímenon and Latin subiectum).

history.meaning: to lay down -> laid down; logical subject, fabricated Tradition

موضوع.notes: Equally natural in formal MSA and casual Jordanian talk (شو الموضوع؟ 'what's going on / what's the matter?', انسى الموضوع 'forget about it').

موظف.etymology: Form II passive participle and noun مُوَظَّف (muwaẓẓaf, 'appointed to an office or post; employee, clerk, official') from وَظَّفَ (waẓẓafa, 'to assign a daily allowance or post, employ'), related to وَظِيفَة (waẓīfa, 'assigned duty, office, job') on the root و-ظ-ف (w-ẓ-f).

history.meaning: appointed to a post; official; employee

morphemes.meaning: assigning a task or post; employment

موظفة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean the clerk (f.).

موعد.etymology: Noun of time and place مَوْعِد (mawʿid, 'appointed time or place, promise, appointment, schedule') derived from وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise, appoint a time') on the Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

موقّع.etymology: Form II passive participle of Arabic وَقَّعَ (waqqaʿa, 'to affix a signature, stamp'), root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

موهبة.etymology: Noun مَوْهِبَة (mawhiba, 'gift, natural endowment, talent') derived from وَهَبَ (wahaba, 'to give, grant, bestow freely') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ه-ب (w-h-b).

مي.etymology: Levantine noun مَيّ / مَيَّة (mayy / mayye, 'water'), evolved from the Classical Arabic diminutive مُوَيْه / مُوَيْهَة (muwayh / muwayha, 'little water') of مَاء (māʾ, 'water') via glide assimilation, from Proto-Semitic *may- ('water'), root م-و-ه (m-w-h).

مية.etymology: Spoken Levantine numeral مِيَّة (miyye, 'one hundred'), reflecting regular medial hamza loss and glide resolution (-iʾa > -iyye) from Classical Arabic مِائَة / مِئَة (miʾa, 'hundred'), from Proto-Semitic *miʾat-.

ميز.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'he recognizes'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

ميزانية.etymology: Abstract noun in -iyya built on مِيزَان (mīzān, 'pair of scales, balance'), itself an instrument noun (مِفْعَال) from root و-ز-ن (w-z-n, 'to weigh'): weighing income against expenditure ('budget').

مين.etymology: Spoken Levantine interrogative pronoun مِين (mīn, 'who?'), developed from Classical Arabic مَنْ (man, 'who?') with vowel lengthening under pause and Aramaic substrate influence, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *man- ('who?').

مينا.etymology: Colloquial Levantine pronunciation مِينا (mīnā) of Classical Arabic مِينَاء (mīnāʾ, 'harbour, port'), borrowed in late antiquity from Ancient Greek λιμένας / λιμήν (liménas / limḗn, 'harbour') via Coptic or Syriac intermediaries with dissimilation of l-m to m-n (or reanalyzed under root و-ن-ي).

ميّز.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean tell apart; distinguish.

مَنَع.etymology: Form I verb مَنَعَ (manaʿa, 'to prevent, block, keep out, withhold, forbid') on the triliteral Semitic root م-ن-ع (m-n-ʿ).

مِشِي.etymology: Levantine Form I verb مِشِي (mišī, 'to walk, go, flow, move along'), reflecting the regular Levantine shift of active intransitive defective verbs to the faʿil vocalism from Classical Arabic مَشَى (mašā, 'to walk, go on foot') on the root م-ش-ي (m-š-y).

نادى.etymology: Form III verb نَادَى (nādā, 'to call out to, summon, call by name') on the root ن-د-و (n-d-w) / ن-د-ي (n-d-y, 'calling out, assembly').

history.meaning: to call out to; summon; call by name

نار.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَار (nār, 'fire'), root ن-و-ر ('light/fire'), cognate with Aramaic נוּרָא (nūrā).

نازل.etymology: Form I active participle نَازِل (nāzil, 'descending, going down; alighting, staying [at an inn or hotel]') from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, alight, lodge') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

ناس.etymology: Collective noun نَاس (nās, 'people, folk, humankind'), formed by apheresis of initial hamza from أُنَاس (ʾunās, 'people'), on the Proto-Semitic root ء-ن-س (ʾ-n-s, 'human, sociable, companion').

ناشف.etymology: Form I active participle نَاشِف (nāšif, 'dry, dried up') from نَشِفَ (našifa, 'to absorb moisture, dry up') on the Semitic root ن-ش-ف (n-š-f).
