ناعم.etymology: Form I active participle نَاعِم (nāʿim, 'soft, smooth, tender, finely powdered') from نَعُمَ (naʿuma) / نَعِمَ (naʿima, 'to be soft, smooth, delicate') on the Semitic root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m).

نافورة.etymology: From Arabic نَافُورَة (nāfūra, 'fountain, water-jet'), derived on the intensive instrument/feature pattern فَاعُولَة from the root ن-ف-ر (n-f-r, 'to spurt, gush forth, spring'). Classic architectural feature of traditional Levantine courtyard houses (بيت عربي) alongside the citrus trees.

ناقص.etymology: Form I active participle نَاقِص (nāqiṣ, 'diminished, lacking, missing, incomplete') from نَقَصَ (naqaṣa, 'to decrease, fall short, lack') on the root ن-ق-ص (n-q-ṣ).

نام.etymology: Form I hollow verb نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep, fall asleep, lie dormant'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *nawām- ('to slumber, doze'), on the root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

ناول.etymology: Form III verb نَاوَلَ (nāwala, 'to hand over, reach out and pass [something to someone]') from نَالَ (nāla, 'to reach, obtain, give') on the hollow root ن-و-ل (n-w-l).

history.meaning: to hand over; pass to someone

ناوي.etymology: Form I active participle نَاوٍ / نَاوِي (nāwī, 'intending, resolving, planning to') from نَوَى (nawā, 'to intend, purpose, resolve upon') on the root ن-و-ي (n-w-y).

نايم.etymology: Spoken Levantine active participle نَايِم (nāyim, 'sleeping, asleep'), reflecting the regular vernacular shift of medial hamza to y in hollow active participles from Classical Arabic نَائِم (nāʾim, 'sleeping'), from نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep'), root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

نتفة.etymology: Noun نُتْفَة / نَتْفَة (nutfa / natfa, 'small tuft plucked with the fingers; tiny bit, pinch, scrap') derived from نَتَفَ (natafa, 'to pluck, pull out [hairs, wool, or a pinch]') on the root ن-ت-ف (n-t-f).

history.meaning: plucked tuft; small pinch or bit

نجار.etymology: Occupational noun نَجَّار (najjār, 'carpenter, joiner, woodworker') on the professional pattern فَعَّال (faʿʿāl) from نَجَرَ (najara, 'to hew, plane, shape wood'), root ن-ج-ر (n-j-r), an ancient Mesopotamian-Semitic craft term cognate with Aramaic ܢܓܪܐ (naggārā) and Akkadian naggārum ('carpenter').

نجح.etymology: Form I verb نَجَحَ (najaḥa, 'to succeed, prosper, turn out well, pass') on the triliteral root ن-ج-ح (n-j-ḥ).

نجمة.etymology: Singulative noun نَجْمَة (najma, 'a star') formed with the singulative suffix ـَة (-a) from the collective noun نَجْم (najm, 'stars, celestial body') on the root ن-ج-م (n-j-m, 'to appear, rise').

نحاس.etymology: Inherited Semitic metal term (*nuḥāš-, 'copper, brass, bronze'), naming the warm yellow-red metal prized by Levantine smiths for keys, trays, and valves.

نخزة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean twinge.

نزل.etymology: Noun نُزُل / نُزْل (nuzul / nuzl, 'lodging prepared for a traveler, guesthouse, inn, hospice') derived from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to alight, dismount, stop for lodging') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

نزّل.etymology: Form II causative verb نَزَّلَ (nazzala, 'to bring down, lower, send down, unload') from نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, go down') on the root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

history.meaning: to send down; bring down; lower

نسبة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean regarding / about.

نسخ.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَسَخَ (nasaḫa, 'to copy out, transcribe, replace'), from the root ن-س-خ (n-s-ḫ, 'to remove, transcribe, supersede'). Historically the core verb for manuscript scribes, it remains the everyday word for copying drawings, keys, and digital files.

نسخة.etymology: From Classical Arabic نُسْخَة (nuskha, 'transcript, copy'), root ن-س-خ (n-s-kh, 'to copy, transcribe').

نسمة.etymology: Singulative noun نَسَمَة / نَسْمَة (nasama / nasma, 'gentle breath of air, breeze') from نَسَمَ (nasama, 'to blow gently [of the wind], breathe softly') on the Proto-Semitic root ن-س-م (n-s-m, 'breath, breeze').

نسي.etymology: Form I defective verb نَسِيَ (nasiya, 'to forget, leave out of mind'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *našay- ('to forget'), on the root ن-س-ي (n-s-y).

نسيم.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَسِيم (nasīm, 'gentle breeze, soft breath of wind'), derived from the root ن-س-م (n-s-m, 'to blow gently, breathe'), cognate with Hebrew נְשָׁמָה (nəšāmā, 'breath, soul'). Beloved in Arabic poetry and everyday conversation for Amman's cool summer evening air.

نشر.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَشَرَ (našara, 'to spread out, unfold, scatter, diffuse'), from the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r, 'to unfold, unroll, saw'). In Levantine household speech, نَشَرَ is the everyday verb for stringing laundry or banners out across a rooftop line, alongside modern 'to publish/post'.

نشرة.etymology: Noun نَشْرَة (našra, 'spreading out, announcement, bulletin, broadcast, weather forecast') derived from نَشَرَ (našara, 'to spread out, unfold, publish, broadcast') on the root ن-ش-ر (n-š-r).

نشف.etymology: Form I intransitive verb نَشِفَ (našifa, 'to dry, become dry, absorb water') on the Semitic root ن-ش-ف (n-š-f).

history.meaning: to absorb water; dry up; become dry

نص.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun نُصّ (nuṣṣ, 'half; middle'), developed by total assimilation of final -f to the preceding emphatic sibilant (-ṣf > -ṣṣ) from Classical Arabic نِصْف (niṣf, 'half'), root ن-ص-ف (n-ṣ-f).

نصاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective نُصَّانِيّ (nuṣṣānī, 'middle, central, situated in the middle'), formed with the augmented relational suffix ـَانِيّ (-āniyy) from نُصّ (nuṣṣ, 'half, middle') < Classical Arabic نِصْف (niṣf), root ن-ص-ف (n-ṣ-f).

نضارة.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean my glasses.

نضافة.etymology: Urban Jordanian/Levantine realization نَضَافَة (naḍāfa) of Classical Arabic نَظَافَة (naẓāfa, 'cleanliness, purity'), verbal noun from the root ن-ظ-ف (n-ẓ-f, 'to be clean, spotless'). Reflects the regular urban Levantine merger of interdental ظ with emphatic stop ض.

نضيف.etymology: Spoken Levantine adjective نْضِيف (nḍīf, 'clean, spotless'), reflecting the regular urban Levantine merger of interdental *ẓ into emphatic stop ḍ from Classical Arabic نَظِيف (naẓīf, 'clean'), root ن-ظ-ف (n-ẓ-f).

نط.etymology: Form I geminate verb نَطَّ (naṭṭa, 'to jump, leap, hop, bound') on the triliteral root ن-ط-ط (n-ṭ-ṭ).

نظارة.etymology: Intensive instrumental feminine noun نَظَّارَة ('eyeglasses, spectacles') coined on the pattern فَعَّالَة from the Semitic root ن-ظ-ر ('look, observe, gaze attentively').

نظر.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic verbal noun نَظَر (naẓar, 'looking, gaze, eyesight, consideration') on the pattern فَعَل (faʿal) of نَظَرَ (naẓara, 'to look at, observe'), inherited from Proto-Semitic root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r, 'to watch, guard').

history.meaning: sight, gaze, attention, point of view

نظر.notes: Appears in everyday expressions like لفت نظرهم ('draw their attention'), بغض النظر ('regardless'), and بنظري ('in my view').

نظرة.etymology: Noun of single instance (ism marra) نَظْرَة (naẓra, 'a single look, glance, gaze') from نَظَرَ (naẓara, 'to look at, gaze, observe') on the Proto-Semitic root ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r).

نظيف.etymology: Stative adjective نَظِيف (naẓīf, 'clean, pure, neat') formed on the pattern فَعِيل (faʿīl) from نَظُفَ (naẓufa, 'to be clean, pure') on the root ن-ظ-ف (n-ẓ-f).

نعم.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic affirmative particle نَعَمْ (naʿam, 'yes, indeed'), traditionally derived from the Semitic root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m, 'pleasantness, ease, favor', compare نِعْمَ niʿma 'how good is...').

نعنع.etymology: Reduplicated aromatic plant noun (نَعْنَع / نَعْنَاع naʿnaʿ) of ancient Semitic heritage, attested across Arabic and Aramaic for garden mint.

نعومة.etymology: From Classical Arabic نُعُومَة (nuʿūma, 'softness, smoothness, tenderness'), abstract verbal noun from the root ن-ع-م (n-ʿ-m, 'to be soft, comfortable, pleasant'), cognate with Hebrew נֹעַם (nōʿam, 'pleasantness'). Preceded by بـ (bi-nʿūme), it serves as an adverb meaning 'gently, smoothly'.

نغمة.etymology: Singulative noun نَغْمَة (naġma, 'musical note, tone, melody, inflection') derived from نَغَمَ (naġama, 'to hum, sing softly, intone') on the root ن-غ-م (n-ġ-m).

نفخ.etymology: Form I verb نَفَخَ (nafaḫa, 'to blow, inflate, puff up, swell'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *napāḫ- ('to blow, breathe upon'), on the root ن-ف-خ (n-f-ḫ).

نفس.etymology: Unvocalized lemma covering Classical Arabic نَفَس (nafas, 'breath, puff of air') and نَفْس (nafs, 'soul, self; same'), both inherited from Proto-Semitic *napš- ('breath, throat, life, self') on the root ن-ف-س (n-f-s).

نقطة.etymology: Noun نُقْطَة (nuqṭa, 'drop [of liquid], dot, point, spot') derived from نَقَطَ (naqaṭa, 'to mark with dots, drip') on the Semitic root ن-ق-ط (n-q-ṭ).

نقل.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) نَقْل (naql, 'carrying across, transfer, transport, relocation, copying') from نَقَلَ (naqala, 'to move, carry from one place to another') on the root ن-ق-ل (n-q-l).

نقّط.etymology: Form II verb نَقَّطَ (naqqaṭa, 'to drip, fall in drops, dot') from نَقَطَ (naqaṭa) and نُقْطَة (nuqṭa, 'drop, dot') on the root ن-ق-ط (n-q-ṭ).

نهار.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic نَهَار (nahār, 'daytime, daylight, day from dawn to dusk'), cognate with Aramaic ܢܗܪܐ / נהورא (nəhōrā, 'light'), from the Semitic root ن-ه-ر (n-h-r, 'to shine brightly, flow abundantly').

نهاية.etymology: Verbal noun نِهَايَة (nihāya, 'end, limit, extremity, conclusion') derived on the pattern فِعَالَة (fiʿāla) from نَهَى (nahā) / اِنْتَهَى (intahā, 'to reach the end, come to a stop') on the root ن-ه-ي (n-h-y).

نهر.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَهْر / نَهَر (nahr, 'river, flowing stream'), Proto-Semitic *nahar-, cognate with Hebrew נָהָר (nāhār).

نوتة.etymology: Borrowed into Arabic from Italian nota ('musical note, written score, memorandum, pocket notebook'), from Latin nota ('mark, sign, musical character, note').

history.meaning: sheet music; musical score; pocket notepad

نور.etymology: From the hollow root ن-و-ر (n-w-r, 'light, illumination, blossom'), related to نار ('fire') and منارة ('lighthouse, minaret').
نور.notes: Appears both as a beloved Arabic given name (نور) and in the classic morning reply صباح النور ('morning of light').

نوع.etymology: From Classical Arabic نَوْع (nawʿ, 'kind, sort, species, manner'), from the hollow root ن-و-ع (n-w-ʿ, 'to sway, branch out into varieties'). Adopted into philosophical, scientific, and everyday Arabic alike as the standard word for 'type' or 'kind'.

نوم.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean to sleep; to bed.

نومة.etymology: Noun of single instance (ism marra) نَوْمَة (nawma, 'a sleep, nap, night's rest') from نَامَ (nāma, 'to sleep') on the hollow root ن-و-م (n-w-m).

history.meaning: a single sleep; nap; night's rest

نَقَل.etymology: Form I verb نَقَلَ (naqala, 'to move, carry from one place to another, transfer, copy') on the triliteral Semitic root ن-ق-ل (n-q-l).

history.meaning: to carry across; move; transfer; copy

نِزِل.etymology: Levantine Form I verb نِزِل (nizil, 'to go down, come down, descend, get off, stay [at a hotel]'), from Classical Arabic نَزَلَ (nazala, 'to descend, alight, lodge') on the Semitic root ن-ز-ل (n-z-l).

history.meaning: to go down; come down; stay at

ها.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic presentative and attentional particle هَا (hā, 'lo!, behold!, here!, ha!'), from Proto-Semitic *hā-.

هات.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic suppletive imperative verb هَاتِ (hāti, 'give!, bring!, hand over!'), historically an old causative imperative formation (with h- for ʾ-) related to آتَى (ʾātā, 'to bring, give') from أَتَى (ʾatā, 'to come') on the Proto-Semitic root ء-ت-ي (ʾ-t-y).

هاد.etymology: Spoken Levantine masculine demonstrative هَاد (hād, 'this, that'), developed from Classical Arabic هٰذَا (hāḏā, 'this [m.]' — compounded of presentative هَا hā + demonstrative ذَا ḏā) with regular urban Levantine shift of interdental *ḏ to stop d and apocope of final vowel.

هادا.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean this; that.

هادي.etymology: Levantine active participle هَادِي (hādī, 'quiet, calm, gentle'), reflecting the regular loss of word-final hamza after -ī from Classical Arabic هَادِئ (hādiʾ, 'calm, quiet, still'), from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, subside, calm down') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هاديك.etymology: Levantine feminine distal demonstrative formed from ها- (ha-) + ذِيك (dhīk, 'that fem.') with colloquial d/dh shift.

هاي.etymology: Jordanian and Levantine feminine singular proximal demonstrative (هَاي hāy, 'this'), reshaped in spoken Levantine from Classical Arabic هٰذِهِ / pausal هٰذِي (hāḏī) by combining the demonstrative presentative prefix هَا- (hā-) with a palatalized feminine ending -ي (-y).
هاي.notes: Colloquial Jordanian/Palestinian/Syrian counterpart of MSA هذه; precedes a definite noun (هاي المدرسة, 'this school') or stands alone as a subject (هاي أول مرة, 'this is the first time').

هب.etymology: From Classical Arabic هَبَّ (habba, 'to blow [of wind], wake up suddenly, flare up'), geminate verb from the root ه-ب-ب (h-b-b, 'blowing wind, sudden rising'). When conjugated with consonant-initial endings in Levantine, the doubled b resolves with -ē- (habbēt 'I/you blew', habb 'it blew').

هبة.etymology: Noun of single instance (اسم مرة) هَبَّة (habba, 'a single gust, sudden puff') formed with -a from the geminate verb هَبَّ (habba, 'to blow'). Very frequent in Jordanian speech in the phrase هبة هوا ('a sudden gust of wind').

هدا.etymology: Levantine noun هَدَا (hadā, 'calm, quietness, gentleness', used especially in عَالهَدَا ʿa-l-hadā 'gently, slowly, quietly'), evolved with loss of final hamza from Classical Arabic هَدْء (hadʾ) / هُدُوء (hudūʾ, 'stillness, calm') from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, quiet'), root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هداك.etymology: Spoken Levantine masculine distal demonstrative هَدَاك (hadāk, 'that [over there]'), from Classical Arabic هٰذَاكَ (hāḏāka, 'that'), compounded of presentative هَا (hā) + demonstrative ذَا (ḏā, with urban Levantine *ḏ > d) + distal suffix ـكَ (-ka).

هدوء.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) هُدُوء (hudūʾ, 'stillness, quietness, calm, peace') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still, subside, grow quiet') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هدول.etymology: Spoken Levantine plural demonstrative هَدُول (hadōl, 'these, those'), compounded of presentative هَا (hā) + plural demonstrative stem ذُول (ḏōl, related to Classical أُولَىٰ ʾulā / هٰؤُلَاءِ hāʾulāʾi, with urban Levantine *ḏ > d).

هدي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean went quiet.

هدية.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean a gift.

هدّى.etymology: Levantine Form II verb هَدَّى (haddā, 'to calm, quiet down, slow down'), reflecting the regular merger of final-hamza verbs into final-yāʾ from Classical Arabic هَدَّأَ (haddaʾa, 'to calm, soothe, quiet') from هَدَأَ (hadaʾa, 'to be still') on the root ه-د-ء (h-d-ʾ).

هذه.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean and this.

هرب.etymology: Form I verb هَرَبَ (haraba, 'to flee, run away, escape') on the triliteral Semitic root ه-ر-ب (h-r-b).

هز.etymology: Form I geminate verb هَزَّ (hazza, 'to shake, rock, nod [the head], vibrate') on the triliteral root ه-ز-ز (h-z-z).

هلأ.etymology: Urban Levantine colloquial adverb (hallaʾ, 'now, right now'), evolved by rapid allegro contraction of هَالْوَقْت (hal-waqt) < Classical Arabic هٰذَا الْوَقْت (hāḏā l-waqt, 'this time'), with assimilation and loss of -w- plus the urban Levantine shift of uvular ق (/q/) to glottal stop أ (/ʾ/).

rootFamily.gloss: now (Syrian/Lebanese orthographic variant keeping etymological ق)
now (parallel Egyptian contraction of ذا الوقت!)

هلأ.notes: Replaces MSA الآن (al-ʾān) in Amman, Damascus, and Beirut speech; at the start of a sentence (هلأ شوفي...), it also works as a conversational discourse marker ('Look / Well, now...').

هلا.etymology: Levantine temporal adverb هَلَّأ / هَلَّق (hallaʾ / hallaq, 'now, right now'), contracted from the phrase هٰذَا الوَقْت (hāḏā l-waqt, 'this time') via هَالْوَقْت (hal-waqt > hallaq).

هلق.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'now'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

هم.etymology: Form I geminate verb هَمَّ (hamma, 'to concern, matter to, worry, occupy the mind') on the triliteral root ه-م-م (h-m-m).

همس.etymology: From Classical Arabic هَمَسَ (hamasa, 'to whisper, murmur, tread softly'), root ه-م-س (h-m-s).

همه.etymology: Spoken Jordanian and Palestinian third-person plural pronoun هُمِّه (humme, 'they'), developed with gemination and final vowel from Classical Arabic هُمْ / هُمُ (hum / humu, 'they'), from Proto-Semitic *humū.

هنا.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun هَنَا (hanā, 'happiness, wholesome pleasure, enjoyment of food and drink', especially in صَحْتَيْن وَهَنَا ṣaḥtēn w-hanā), apocopated without final hamza from Classical Arabic هَنَاء (hanāʾ, 'wholesomeness, felicity, pleasure') from هَنِئَ (haniʾa, 'to be wholesome and pleasant') on the root ه-ن-ء (h-n-ʾ).

هناك.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic locative adverb هُنَاكَ (hunāka, 'there, over there'), formed from proximal هُنَا (hunā, 'here') + distal suffix ـكَ (-ka).

هنيك.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'there'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

هو.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic third-person masculine singular pronoun هُوَ (huwa, 'he, it'), from Proto-Semitic *huʾa.

هوا.etymology: Spoken Levantine noun هَوَا (hawā, 'air, breeze, wind, weather'), with regular loss of word-final hamza after a long vowel from Classical Arabic هَوَاء (hawāʾ, 'air, atmosphere, breeze') on the root ه-و-ي (h-w-y).

هواية.etymology: From Arabic هِوَايَة (hiwāya, 'hobby, amateur pursuit, fondness'), derived from the root ه-و-ي (h-w-y, 'to desire, love, incline toward'). Alongside هاوٍ ('amateur, hobbyist'), it became the universal Arabic word for a recreational pastime.

هوف.etymology: Expressive onomatopoeic interjection (hūf / hōf) imitating the rushing breath of wind or a relieved exhale, parallel to Levantine أُوف / أفّ. Used conversationally in storytelling to dramatize a sudden gust sweeping across an open terrace.

هون.etymology: Spoken Levantine locative adverb هُون (hōn, 'here'), contracted from Classical Arabic هَاهُنَا (hā-hunā, 'right here' — presentative هَا hā + locative هُنَا hunā) via *hāhun > hōn.

هي.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic third-person feminine singular pronoun هِيَ (hiya, 'she, it'), from Proto-Semitic *šiʾa / *hiʾa.

هيك.etymology: Spoken Levantine adverb of manner هَيْك / هِيك (hēk, 'like this, thus, so'), contracted from Classical Arabic هٰكَذَا (hākaḏā, 'thus, in this way') or compounded from demonstrative هَاي (hāy, 'this') + comparative/distal كَ (ka).

هيه.etymology: Expressive colloquial interjection used across Levantine Arabic to call attention, parallel to Classical Arabic هَيَّا / هَيْ.

هَيّ.etymology: Spoken Levantine presentative particle هَيّ (hayy, 'here is!, look!'), formed by fusing the presentative particle هَا (hā, 'lo!, behold!') with the third-person pronoun هِيَ / هُوَ (hiya / huwa) or demonstrative element.

وإلا.etymology: Compound conjunction وَإِلَّا (wa-ʾillā, 'and if not; otherwise, or else'), composed of coordinating وَ (wa-, 'and') + conditional إِنْ (ʾin, 'if') + negative لَا (lā, 'not').

history.meaning: and if not; otherwise; or else

واحد.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic numeral and adjective وَاحِد (wāḥid, 'one, single, sole, same'), formed on the pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) from the Proto-Semitic root و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d, 'one, alone, single').

وارم.etymology: Form I active participle وَارِم (wārim, 'swollen, puffed up') from وَرِمَ (warima, 'to swell, become swollen') on the Semitic root و-ر-م (w-r-m).

واسع.etymology: Form I active participle وَاسِع (wāsiʿ, 'wide, broad, spacious, roomy') from وَسِعَ (wasiʿa) / وَسُعَ (wasuʿa, 'to be wide, spacious, ample') on the Semitic root و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ).

واصل.etymology: Form I active participle وَاصِل (wāṣil, 'arriving, reaching, connected') from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to arrive, reach, join') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

واضح.etymology: Form I active participle وَاضِح (wāḍiḥ, 'clear, plain, evident, distinct') from وَضَحَ (waḍaḥa, 'to be clear, become plain or visible') on the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ).

واطي.etymology: Levantine active participle وَاطِي (wāṭī, 'low [in height, level, or volume]'), reflecting the regular loss of word-final hamza after -ī from Classical Arabic وَاطِئ (wāṭiʾ, 'treading; low-lying, depressed [ground]'), from وَطِئَ (waṭiʾa, 'to tread underfoot, level') on the root و-ط-ء (w-ṭ-ʾ).

وافق.etymology: Form III verb وَافَقَ (wāfaqa, 'to agree with, approve, consent to, suit') on the triliteral root و-ف-ق (w-f-q).

واقف.etymology: Form I active participle وَاقِف (wāqif, 'standing, stopped, stationary, parked') from وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop, halt') on the root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

والله.etymology: Univerbation of the Classical Arabic oath phrase وَٱللّٰهِ (wa-llāhi, 'by God!'), combining the jurative preposition وَ- (wa-, 'by [in oaths]', governing the genitive) + ٱللّٰه (Allāh, 'God', from root ء-ل-ه).

rootFamily.gloss: oh God! (also source of يلا, 'let's go!')

والله.notes: Ubiquitous across registers: uttered earnestly to vouch for the truth (والله ما حكيت إشي, 'honestly I didn't say anything') or with rising pitch (والله؟, 'oh really?').

وتد.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَتِد / وَتَد (watid / watad, 'peg, tent-pin, stake'), cognate with Hebrew יָתֵד (yāṯēḏ, 'peg, tent-pin') and Aramaic יַתְדָא. Reflecting shared West Semitic nomadic and architectural vocabulary, it applies to any wooden or iron peg used to anchor cords.

وتر.etymology: Ancient Semitic noun وَتَر ('bowstring; musical string', plural أَوْتَار) from the root و-ت-ر ('draw taut'). From early lutes and qanuns to modern pianos, أوتار names the stretched strings whose vibration produces musical pitch.

وجع.etymology: Verbal noun وَجَع (wajaʿ, 'pain, ache, soreness') from وَجِعَ (wajiʿa, 'to ache, feel pain') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ج-ع (w-j-ʿ).

وجه.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَجْه (wajh, 'face, countenance, front, top surface, side') on the triliteral Semitic root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

وجود.etymology: Classical Arabic verbal noun (maṣdar) وُجُود (wujūd, 'being found, presence, existence') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) of وَجَدَ / passive وُجِدَ (wujida, 'to be found, exist'), initial-weak Semitic root و-ج-د (w-j-d).

history.meaning: to be found -> presence, philosophical existence

وجود.notes: Equally common in philosophical MSA and warm everyday Jordanian phrases like وجودك مريح ('having you around is comforting').

وجّه.etymology: Form II denominal/causative verb وَجَّهَ (wajjaha, 'to turn [something] toward, point, aim, direct') derived from وَجْه (wajh, 'face, front, direction') on the root و-ج-ه (w-j-h).

history.meaning: to turn toward; direct; aim; point

وحدة.etymology: Spoken Levantine feminine singular of واحد ('one'), pronounced وَحْدَة (waḥde), contracted by unstressed vowel syncope from Classical Arabic وَاحِدَة (wāḥida), built on the Semitic initial-weak root و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d, 'oneness, being single').

history.meaning: one (f.); a girl/woman; with الـ (الوَحْدَة), generic 'one / a girl'

rootFamily.gloss: (MSA wuḥda / waḥda) unity; loneliness; curriculum unit

وحدة.notes: Do not confuse colloquial وَحْدَة (waḥde, 'one [female] / a girl', as in ولا وحدة 'not a single one' or لازم الوحدة تنتبه 'a girl must be careful') with MSA وَحْدَة (waḥda, 'loneliness / unity') spelled identically without vowels!

ورا.etymology: Spoken Levantine preposition وَرَا (warā, 'behind, after, past'), with regular loss of word-final hamza after a long vowel from Classical Arabic وَرَاءَ (warāʾa, 'behind, beyond') on the root و-ر-ي (w-r-y).

ورد.etymology: Collective noun وَرْد (ward, 'roses, blossoms, flowers'), an ancient borrowing via Aramaic ܘܪܕܐ (wardā) from Old Iranian *wrda- / Middle Persian *ward ('rose, flower').

ورشة.etymology: Borrowed into Egyptian and Levantine Arabic وَرْشَة (warša, 'workshop, repair shop, construction site') in the nineteenth century from English workshop.

ورق.etymology: Collective noun وَرَق (waraq, 'tree leaves, foliage; sheets of paper'), inherited from Proto-Semitic *waraq- ('green foliage, leaf') on the root و-ر-ق (w-r-q).

ورقة.etymology: Singulative noun وَرَقَة (waraqa, 'a single leaf; a sheet of paper, slip, note') formed with the singulative suffix ـَة (-a) from the collective وَرَق (waraq, 'leaves, paper') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ر-ق (w-r-q).

history.meaning: a leaf; a sheet of paper

ورقي.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean paper (adj.).

ورم.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean the swelling.

ورنيش.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean the varnish.

وزع.etymology: Form II verb وَزَّعَ (wazzaʿa, 'to divide into shares, distribute, hand out, assign') from وَزَعَ (wazaʿa, 'to restrain, apportion') on the root و-ز-ع (w-z-ʿ).

وزن.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) وَزْن (wazn, 'weighing, weight, measure, meter') from وَزَنَ (wazana, 'to weigh') on the Semitic root و-ز-ن (w-z-n).

وزّع.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean and hand out.

وسط.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَسَط / وَسْط (wasaṭ / wasṭ, 'middle, center, midst') on the triliteral root و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ, 'to be in the middle').

وسطاني.etymology: Levantine relational adjective وَسْطَانِيّ (wasṭānī, 'middle, central'), formed with the augmented positional suffix ـَانِيّ (-āniyy) from وَسَط (wasaṭ, 'middle, center') on the root و-س-ط (w-s-ṭ).

وسع.etymology: Form I verb وَسِعَ (wasiʿa, 'to be wide enough for, hold, contain, have room for') on the Proto-Semitic root و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ).

history.meaning: to hold; accommodate; have room for

وسيم.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَسِيم (wasīm, 'handsome, having goodly features'), root و-س-م (w-s-m, 'mark, comeliness').

وش.etymology: Levantine phonological reduction of Classical Arabic وَجْه (wajh, 'face'), via assimilation wajh to wihh and wishsh.

وصفة.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَصْفَة (waṣfa, 'description, prescription, recipe'), verbal noun of وَصَفَ (waṣafa, 'to describe').

وصل.etymology: Form I verb وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to arrive, reach, join, connect') on the Semitic root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

وصلة.etymology: Noun وَصْلَة (waṣla, 'link, joint, connection, pipe fitting, short musical piece') derived from وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, connect') on the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l).

وصول.etymology: From Classical Arabic وُصُول (wuṣūl, 'arrival, reaching, joining'), the standard فُعُول verbal noun of وَصَلَ (waṣala, 'to join, reach, arrive'), from the root و-ص-ل (w-ṣ-l, 'connection, arrival'). Used across all registers for the arrival of guests, trains, or packages.

وضع.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic verbal noun وَضْع (waḍʿ, 'placing, laying down, posture') on the pattern فَعْل (faʿl) of وَضَعَ (waḍaʿa, 'to put down, set'), initial-weak root و-ض-ع (w-ḍ-ʿ), extended in modern MSA and colloquial Arabic to 'state of affairs, situation'.
وضع.notes: Everyday Jordanian greeting/check-in: كيف الوضع؟ ('how are things / what's the situation?'), or هاد الوضع مو طبيعي ('this situation isn't normal').

وضوح.etymology: Form I verbal noun (maṣdar) وُضُوح (wuḍūḥ, 'clarity, plainness, distinctness') on the pattern فُعُول (fuʿūl) from وَضَحَ (waḍaḥa, 'to be clear, plain, evident') on the root و-ض-ح (w-ḍ-ḥ).

وطّى.etymology: Form II verb from Arabic root و-ط-أ (waṭuʾa, 'to be low'), meaning to make low, lower, or turn down.

وظيفة.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic وَظِيفَة (waẓīfa, 'fixed daily ration, allotted duty, official post') on the nominal pattern فَعِيلَة (faʿīla) from the triliteral root و-ظ-ف (w-ẓ-f, 'to assign a regular share or task').

morphemes.meaning: assign a regular duty or ration

وظيفة.notes: Crucial register split: in MSA and Gulf/Egyptian Arabic وظيفة primarily means 'job / employment' (while homework is واجب), whereas in Jordanian, Syrian, and Lebanese schools وظيفة is the everyday word for 'homework'.

وعد.etymology: Form I verbal noun وَعْد (waʿd, 'promise, pledge, word') from وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise') on the Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

وفى.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'I keep/fulfill'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

وفّر.etymology: Form II verb وَفَّرَ (waffara, 'to make abundant, spare, save [money, time, or effort], economize') from وَفَرَ (wafara, 'to be abundant, ample, complete') on the root و-ف-ر (w-f-r).

وقار.etymology: Noun وَقَار (waqār, 'dignity, gravity, calm composure') from وَقُرَ (waqura, 'to be grave, dignified, staid, heavy') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ق-ر (w-q-r, 'to be heavy, honored').

وقت.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَقْت (waqt, 'time, appointed moment, season') on the triliteral Semitic root و-ق-ت (w-q-t).

وقع.etymology: Form I verb وَقَعَ (waqaʿa, 'to fall, drop, tumble, happen, occur') on the triliteral root و-ق-ع (w-q-ʿ).

وقف.etymology: Form I verb وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop, come to a halt') on the triliteral root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

وقور.etymology: From Classical Arabic وَقُور (waqūr, 'sedate, dignified, composed'), root و-ق-ر (w-q-r, 'gravity, reverence').

وقّع.etymology: This word is derived from the Arabic root. It is commonly used in everyday Levantine and Jordanian spoken Arabic to mean you signed.

وقّف.etymology: Form II causative verb وَقَّفَ (waqqafa, 'to cause to stand or stop, halt, park') from وَقَفَ (waqafa, 'to stand, stop') on the root و-ق-ف (w-q-f).

ولا.etymology: Unvocalized conjunction covering Classical and Levantine وَلَا (wa-lā, 'and not, nor, not even', from وَ wa- 'and' + لَا lā 'not') as well as the Levantine disjunctive question conjunction وَلَّا (wallā, 'or', contracted from وَإِلَّا wa-ʾillā 'and if not').

history.meaning: nor, not even; and if not

ولد.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic وَلَد (walad, 'child, boy, son, offspring') from وَلَدَ (walada, 'to give birth, bear, beget') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ل-د (w-l-d).

ويل.etymology: Continues Classical Arabic exclamatory noun of calamity وَيْل (wayl, 'woe, ruin, affliction'), expanded from the primary Semitic lamentation interjection وَيْ (way, 'alas!, woe!').
ويل.notes: In Jordanian speech, يا ويلك مني! ('you're in big trouble with me!') and يا ويل البنت اللي... ('heaven help the girl who...') are vivid dramatic warnings.

وين.etymology: Spoken Levantine interrogative adverb وَيْن (wēn, 'where?'), formed by fusing coordinating وَ (wa-) with Classical Arabic أَيْنَ (ʾayna, 'where?'), from Proto-Semitic *ʾayna.

وَعَد.etymology: Form I verb وَعَدَ (waʿada, 'to promise, give one's word') on the Proto-Semitic root و-ع-د (w-ʿ-d).

يا.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic vocative particle يَا (yā, 'O!, hey!'), from Proto-Semitic *yā.

ياسمين.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Persian *yāsamīn* ('jasmine flower'), fragrant climbing shrub cultivated across Levantine courtyards for centuries.
ياسمين.notes: From Arabic and Persian the word entered medieval Latin and French *jasmin*, giving English 'jasmine'.

يد.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *yad- ('hand, arm, handle'), grammatically feminine because body parts in pairs are feminine in Arabic.
يد.notes: In spoken Jordanian, 'hand' is pronounced إيد (īd, plural إيدين), while يد (yadd) also names a door handle or tool grip.

يدوي.etymology: Nisba adjective formed from Arabic يَد (yad, 'hand') with the historical glide -aw- (يَدَوِيّ), Semitic root ي-د-ي.

يسار.etymology: From an ancient Semitic root for 'left'. Widely used in Levantine Arabic.

يسلموا.etymology: Levantine gratitude expression يِسْلَمُوا (yislamū, 'thank you!', literally 'may they [your hands] be kept safe and well!'), elliptical for يِسْلَمُوا إِيدَيْك (yislamū ʾīdēk), third-person plural optative imperfect of سَلِمَ (salima, 'to be safe, sound, unharmed') on the Proto-Semitic root س-ل-م (s-l-m).

history.meaning: may they be safe and sound

يعني.etymology: Originally the third-person masculine singular imperfect of عنى ('to mean, intend', root ع-ن-ي), literally 'it means'. In spoken Levantine Arabic it grammaticalized into a versatile discourse marker ('so, that is, I mean').
يعني.notes: Learners hear يعني both as a literal verb ('that means') and as a natural conversational bridge.

يلا.etymology: Ubiquitous Arabic hortatory interjection يَلَّا (yallā, 'come on!, let's go!'), contracted from the vocative invocation يَا اللّٰه (yā llāh, 'O God!').

يمكن.etymology: Impersonal third-person masculine singular imperfect verb يُمْكِن (yumkin, literally 'it is possible', used adverbially as 'maybe, perhaps') from Form IV أَمْكَنَ (ʾamkana, 'to be possible, enable') on the root م-ك-ن (m-k-n).

يمين.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic يَمِين (yamīn, 'right hand, right side; oath'), from Proto-Semitic *yamīn- ('right hand, right side') on the root ي-م-ن (y-m-n).

يوم.etymology: Inherited from Classical Arabic يَوْم (yawm, 'day'), from Proto-Semitic *yawm- ('day') on the root ي-و-م (y-w-m).

يوميا.etymology: Adverbial accusative يَوْمِيًّا (yawmiyyan, 'daily, every day') formed from the relational adjective يَوْمِيّ (yawmiyy, 'daily'), itself from يَوْم (yawm, 'day') + nisba suffix ـِيّ (-iyy) + adverbial accusative ending ـًا (-an), root ي-و-م (y-w-m).
